# Topic Inventory

Concepts to cover, ordered by complexity. Each session draws from these tiers.

> Mirrored from the Topic Inventory section of `COURSE_PROGRAM.md` on the repo's `feat/session-4-deck` branch, 2026-11-02 (`e0f75d2`, no PR yet). The standalone tier notes (`fundamentals.md`, `planning_and_review.md`, etc.) no longer exist.

## [Diego] Tier 1: Fundamentals → [[sessions/session-1/session-1|Session 1]]
- **Responsibility is the starting point**: accountability stays with the person, not the AI. "The agent wrote it" is not an excuse.
- The AI-assisted coding spectrum (overview)
  - History: https://www.coderabbit.ai/blog/a-very-brief-history-of-ai-coding-from-copilot-to-next-gen-agents
     - 2017: **Paper:  Attention Is All You Need paper introduced the Transformer**, the architecture that made modern large language models possible.
     - 2022: 
       - **(Junio) Github Copilot (Tab Completions)**: Copilot officially becomes generally available to individual developers as a commercial product, standardizing ghost-text style code completions.
       - **(Noviembre) ChatGPT** -- OpenAI releases ChatGPT (GPT-3.5). While built as a general conversational model, developers rapidly adopt it to write, debug, explain code snippets, and scaffold applications via natural language chat.
     - 2023
       - **Cursor:** A dedicated VS Code fork designed from the ground up for LLM integration, deep codebase indexing, and contextual code editing. 
       - **Copilot Chat:** GitHub announces Copilot X, integrating ChatGPT-style sidebar chat and inline conversational editing directly inside the editor.
    - 2024
       - **Cursor Introduces Composer Mode**: Cursor breaks past single-file assistance with the introduction of multi-file reasoning and "Composer", allowing the agent to create and edit entire codebases simultaneously based on high-level instructions.
       - **Windsurf**, a standalone AI-native IDE designed around "Cascade" and agentic flows, emphasizing bidirectional real-time awareness between the developer and the agent across the whole workspace.
    - 2025
      - Anthropic Launches **Claude Code**. Operating primarily as an agentic CLI tool in the terminal, it executes bash commands, searches repositories, edits multiple files, runs tests, and fixes build issues autonomously.
    - 2025 / 2026
      - OpenCode, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, GLM Coding, Kimi CLI, Pi

- Generative AI: what it is, where LLMs sit inside it
- LLM fundamentals: how they work at a practical level — tokens, context windows, probability, why hallucinations happen.
- The model landscape: Anthropic (Claude), OpenAI (GPT), Z.ai (GLM), Moonshot AI (Kimi). Reading a model page: modalities, context window, price. OpenAI's model-comparison page as a way to teach the base concepts in one pass.
- Tokens as the unit of everything: input, output, and price. Multimodality — images and audio become tokens too.
- Pricing shapes: per-token (API) vs subscription, and when each makes sense.
- Context window as finite working memory — and the context rot rule: **try to don't go past 50%** of what the model supports.
- **Context hygiene as operations**, named in the Session 1 hands-on and used from day one: `/session` (tokens and cost so far), `/new` (clean context for an unrelated task), `/compact` (summarize the old part of a long task), `/tree` (rewind to before the agent dug the hole). Four commands, not a topic — the mechanism is Session 5's.
- Chat vs agent: a chat returns text and you execute; an agent executes in a loop (reads, runs, edits, checks, retries).
- Vibe coding: prompt-and-accept workflow. Talk with the agent, don't open files — focus entirely on the output. Working definition: *programar sin pensar que el código existe*.
- Analyzing AI output: what did it actually produce?
- Code quality awareness: dead code? inconsistent patterns? missing tests? mantainability?
- Comprehension debt: you shipped code you don't understand
- Anatomy of a coding agent (brief intro): LLM + tools + harness — just enough vocabulary to use these terms in later sessions
  - Tool: a function the LLM can invoke (read file, run shell, edit code)
  - Coding agent: an LLM that takes actions on a codebase via tools in a loop
  - Harness: the program wrapping the LLM (context management, tool dispatch, permissions). Pi is a harness.
  - The catalogue by environment: web (Lovable, v0, Bolt, Claude Code web), desktop (Claude Code desktop), terminal (Claude Code, Codex, Pi, opencode)


## [Agus] Tier 2: Planning & Review → [[sessions/session-2/session-2|Session 2]]
- AI gets you to something that works, but decisions and details are missing, and you don't know where or how many
- Planning as explore → design → document, then implement from the document. The design can be as light or as thorough as needed; more design costs time up front and buys less rework and more understanding of what comes out
- The design document as a first-class artifact: drafted, read and corrected before it is saved, annotated, versioned, committed with the code. It can carry diagrams, not only prose. `@plannotator/pi-extension` as a small help (*una ayudita*) for annotating it (`/plannotator-annotate`) and the diff (`/plannotator-review`)
- Plan mode (`pi --plan`) as an existing mechanism students can try, not a required step. The harness restricts the toolset to read/search while it is on (seeds Tier 3's permissions/extension-points material)
- Review is getting harder (more code, and code nobody on the team wrote) and the industry is still looking for ways to do it. Two of them used here: moving review earlier, into the design, and verifying that the result works. Reading the diff to understand it and check it against the design
- Testing: the test pyramid (unit, integration, e2e) as vocabulary, and the agent can write all of them. Unattended, you don't know if they test the right thing. Deciding the cases before the code with a simplified Classification Tree Method, each case marked as covered by a test, by the agent's verification, or both
- Verification: the agent exercises what it built. Against an API with `curl`; on screen with a browser-driving CLI (`agent-browser`), introduced in one line since tools are Tier 3's. Verifying becomes the fifth stop after explore → design → document → code
- Debugging AI-generated code: read it yourself before asking for a fix

## [Diego] Tier 3: Tooling & Skills → [[sessions/session-3/session-3|Session 3]]

> Prerequisite, not content: **Pi is installed in Session 1**, and Session 2 adds the Plannotator extension and the `agent-browser` CLI; `pi-subagents` is installed in Session 3's hands-on, where subagents are taught. Tier 3 goes deeper on the harness — it does not introduce it. `AGENTS.md` **is** introduced here from scratch: the Session 1 step that had students write one was dropped, and Session 2 does not touch it.
>
> **Subagents are taught here** (moved back while building Session 3's deck, PR #16): the primitive closes the theory and the hands-on installs `pi-subagents`. Session 4 then shows them in use inside a real run, and Session 5 opens the mechanism.
>
> **Worktrees are out of the course**, not relocated. They were only ever a one-line mention riding along with subagents, no session's hands-on needs them, and Session 2's git block no longer names them either. Cut rather than parked.

- Tools deep dive: what tools are, how the LLM calls them, examples from Pi's toolbelt (read, write, edit, bash, grep, find, ls). Why tools are the unit of capability.
- Harness deep dive: what Pi provides as a harness — context management, tool dispatch, permissions, extension points. Comparison with other harnesses (Claude Code, Cursor, Aider, OpenCode). Why the harness matters as much as the model.
- Custom instructions: `AGENTS.md` from scratch — what it is, the loading order across directories, rules files. Students arrive with the *motivation* for it from Session 2's homework ("what did you have to explain to the agent more than once?"), not with a file.
- Skills / slash commands: teaching AI reusable behaviors. **[Agent Skills](https://agentskills.io/) is an open standard**, not a Pi feature — a folder with a `SKILL.md`, published by Anthropic and adopted across Claude Code, Cursor, Copilot/VS Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, OpenCode and Pi. The three-stage loading taught here is the standard's *progressive disclosure*. Worth one sentence in class: it's the first artefact of the course that transfers to whatever tool the student uses next — and a small rehearsal of what Session 6 makes students verify by hand.
- MCP / external tools: extending the harness — the LLM gains new tools at runtime
- Documentation tools (e.g. [context7](https://context7.com/), [context-hub](https://github.com/andrewyng/context-hub)): fetching up-to-date library docs so the AI works with accurate references instead of guessing
- Subagents, the primitive: a whole job sent to a separate context, so only its conclusion comes back. Pi doesn't ship them; `pi-subagents` adds them

## [Agus] Tier 4: Context Engineering → [[sessions/session-4/session-4|Session 4]]
- `AGENTS.md` as an index: what the agent needs every turn stays in it, and the rest sits one link away in the project's docs and wiki. What goes where: `AGENTS.md` (every turn), `docs/` (how each part of the system works and why), the wiki (how to work in this code)
- Problem and solution: the same need admits many solutions. Starting from the solution means deciding without having considered the problem, and inheriting the agent's average answer for every decision left open. It is the old split between requirements and design, and it matters with or without AI
- Defining the problem is mapping reality: actors, entities, processes, rules. Often a product team's job; in a student project, nobody else does it
- Defining the solution: model, flows, states, components, screens and prototypes, each decision with its reason
- Letting the agent ask the decisions one at a time, instead of asking it for the document. Delegating the writing is fine; delegating the thinking is the failure mode
- Living documents: doc → code → review → reconcile. The review checks that what was built is what was decided, and catches what the implementation surfaced that the design didn't cover; reconciling brings the doc back in line with the code, and the next change reads it while exploring
- Subagents in use: one context per job (scouts while exploring, one implementer per repository, one reviewer per facet). The brief is all a subagent knows, and the docs are the ground truth they share. The primitive is Tier 3's, the mechanism Tier 5's
- Cognitive debt and cognitive surrender: the cost of repeatedly delegating reasoning to the AI, and adopting its decisions as your own
- Cost and limits: money, context and attention; when NOT to use AI, skill atrophy, and ownership (understand, decide, discuss, maintain). This tier closes the *"how do I work well with this thing?"* arc, so the judgment material lives here. The full-course retrospective belongs to Tier 6

## [Agus] Tier 5: Harness Internals → [[sessions/session-5/session-5|Session 5]]

> **The spine: teach the concept, use Pi as the specimen.** Every topic here is a design decision *any* harness has to make; Pi is the one we can open, not the one being sold. That rehearses Tier 6's model swap a week early. The failure mode of this tier is turning into a tour of Pi's features.

- What a harness is, revisited from Tier 1: interface, agent loop, tools/memory/context, model. An LLM alone predicts tokens and can do nothing; the harness connects it to the world.
- **The other harnesses, as axes rather than a ranking**: open vs. closed source, what ships built in vs. what you add, whether there is an extension surface and how deep it reaches, who controls the system prompt. The questions to ask the next tool they pick up. **No comparison table** — comparing harnesses in the abstract is useless to someone who has used one.
- The agent loop, step by step, with the extension points on the arrows: `session_start`, `resources_discover`, `input`, `before_agent_start`, `turn_start`, `context`, the model call, `tool_call`, `tool_result`, `turn_end`, `agent_end`, `session_shutdown`. Every moment is subscribable, and from there you block, modify or inject. **This is where Tier 2's plan mode finally gets its mechanism**: `tool_call` → `{ block: true }`.
- Harness architecture as layers, and the idea that you use only the ones you need. Pi's four packages: unified model API, generic agent loop, coding layer, terminal UI.
- **Sessions as a tree, not a list**: entries with `id` and `parentId`, the active leaf, the whole tree in one file. Why `/tree` is cheap — you move a pointer, you don't delete. Tier 1 sold it as the antidote to cascading errors; here it gets its reason.
- **Steering vs. follow-up**: when does new information reach an agent that is already running? Interrupt mid-stream, wait for it to settle, or queue for the next turn. Every harness decides this; most hide it.
- **Three ways to give a model a tool**, and the tradeoffs: an **extension** (reaches harness internals, works in that harness only), a **CLI** (simplest, portable to any harness with a shell, no auth story, and the agent has to learn it exists — which is what `AGENTS.md` is for), **MCP** (for tools other people consume: distribution, auth, remote services, paid for in context). The question that decides it is who the consumer is.
- **Subagents, the mechanism** (the use case is Tier 4's): a separate context with its own transcript, whose entire result returns to the parent as one message. The honest reason is context economy, not "more AI".
- **Compaction**, the debt Tier 1 assigned here: the trigger (`contextTokens > contextWindow - reserveTokens`), the algorithm (walk back to `keepRecentTokens`, cut, summarize the older half in a structured format, store the summary with the first kept entry), and the two consequences — it is lossy and it is another model call, and it is interceptable.
- **Run modes**: interactive, headless one-shot, embedded as a library, served behind a protocol. The agent loop is a library and the terminal is one of its interfaces. Why CI agents, bots and in-browser agents exist.
- **Security, generalized**: threat models (prompt injection from repo content, a malicious extension/skill/MCP server, the agent's own destructive mistakes, credential exfiltration), permission models as a design space, and the sandbox ladder (none → in-process → container → micro-VM → separate machine). The counterintuitive argument worth stating: **a partial sandbox is worse than none**, because it reads as a boundary while still resting on your shell, filesystem, package managers and credentials. Real isolation comes from the OS.

## [Diego] Tier 6: Open Source Models & HPC → [[sessions/session-6/session-6|Session 6]]

> 🔴 **TO REVIEW** — Claude-generated, not yet reviewed by Diego.

- **Open source vs. open weights**: open weights means you can download and run them; open source in the strong sense means you could reproduce the model (training code + data information). Nearly everything marketed as "open source AI" is open weights — the binary, not the recipe.
- **Licences**, where that distinction gets consequences: standard software licences (Apache 2.0, MIT) vs. bespoke licences with usage restrictions and scale clauses (Llama community licence, Gemma terms) vs. restrictions on the output itself. The three questions to answer before shipping: commercial use? redistribute a fine-tune? who owns the generations?
- Honest about the capability gap on long-horizon agentic work and reliable tool calling. **The control-spectrum table was cut** when the theory block moved to Copes's arc — the tradeoffs are still named, through his five reasons and his list of what open weights do not guarantee.
- **Is an open model good enough to be the engine of a serious project?** No longer a taught block — 150 minutes do not hold it. It survives as written material in the exercise (Raschka's measurements, and when open source is the right call), and the VRAM figure goes to Agus to close his demo. The line worth keeping wherever it lands: the bottleneck is usually reliable tool calling, not the ability to write code.
- **Running one on your own hardware**, made concrete: **Agus's 15-minute demo** — a portable eGPU on the desk, Ollama on CUDA, and the quantization arithmetic from the theory checked against 16 GB of real VRAM. He shows, the room watches; it is not an endpoint students connect to.
- What it takes to run one: what a download actually gets you (safetensors vs. GGUF, tokenizer, runtime, the token loop), quantization and its cost to structured output — i.e. to tool calling — and the OpenAI-compatible endpoint that lets any harness point anywhere. **The local-vs-serving runtime distinction is no longer taught as a block**; the guest owns batching in his slot, and the contrast has a real referent in the room instead: CCAD runs **vLLM** behind its gateway because it serves many users, while Agus's demo runs **Ollama** on one card.
- **The context window is paid for in VRAM, not just declared.** The best single moment of the theory arc, and it needs the demo to land: `30B × 4 bits ≈ 15 GB` of weights against a 16 GB card reads as "it just fits" and does not, because the KV cache lives there too. It returns twice more — as `--max-model-len` on CCAD's side, and as `contextWindow` in the student's own JSON.
- The OpenAI-compatible endpoint as the interoperability story: why a harness can point at a different model by adding a provider to its config. This is the technical bridge from Tier 5.
- **The inference gateway.** CCAD is reached through a **LiteLLM** proxy exposing an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, and Pi gets there with a provider entry in `~/.pi/agent/models.json` — no SSH, no scheduler, no tunnel. Swapping the model is a config file. Two things that fall out of it and are worth teaching: the context window turns out to be a startup parameter somebody chose (server-side here, chosen by the student with `-c` in the local track), and **a gateway is also a third party** — "runs on UNC hardware" is not the same as "nobody sees my prompts".
- Shared-resource etiquette, in one line when the hands-on is released: people are running their theses on those machines. **Cluster mechanics are out of the course** — login vs. compute node, the scheduler, modules, port forwarding are internals of a multi-user inference service; the guest touches them lightly and that's it.
- **CCAD (Centro de Computación de Alto Desempeño, UNC)**: a 60-minute guest talk by Ale Silva, and the programme is his — an introduction to HPC and why clusters are needed; UNC Supercómputo's history, clusters and metrics, and where it stands against the region and the world; the experience of deploying models on limited hardware and turning a working test into a stable multi-user service; and how to use CCAD's resources, from requesting an account to making a first call to their models. Most students don't know UNC runs an HPC center they can use. **Access is the takeaway that outlives the course** — and it is explicitly the road back *after* the course, not today's access, which runs on a key Diego hands out. His third point is where LiteLLM and vLLM get named by the person who chose them, fifteen minutes before students type them into `models.json`. Cluster mechanics stay out — light touch only.
- Supply chain and self-hosting risk: what you trust when you download multi-gigabyte binary weights; how self-hosting removes a third party and adds you as the operator.
- When open source is the right call: sensitive data, cost-dominated volume, research reproducibility, offline work, studying the model itself — versus wanting the best coding agent today with no ops capacity.

## Cross-cutting: Security & Trust (woven throughout)
Not a dedicated session, but surfaced where relevant:
- **Session 1**: security issues found during code analysis (common vulnerabilities in AI output)
- **Session 2**: none dedicated — a security smell gets named in passing if one shows up in the demo's diff
- **Session 3**: sandboxing, permission models, why tools have allowlists/denylists
- **Session 4**: none dedicated — trust boundaries, prompt injection and supply chain moved out of this session and **landed in Session 5**, which now closes the thread with a block of its own
- **Session 5**: the block that closes the thread. Threat models (prompt injection from repo content, malicious extensions/skills/MCP servers, the agent's own destructive mistakes, credential exfiltration), permission models as a design space, and the sandbox ladder. Placed after the hands-on so it lands on an extension they just wrote and installed themselves.
- **Session 6**: self-hosting makes *you* the operator — runtime, patching, machine, quality — and "local" does not automatically mean private, since the agent still calls out. **Narrowed deliberately**: the open-weight block now follows Copes's arc, which covers those two and not the model supply chain or injection, so the session no longer promises them.

# Session 4: Context Engineering

Reworked 2026-11-02 into a **live run with a concept-only deck**. Agus builds a new kurasu feature, a chat in the featured session's classroom, with the mahou skills (explore, shape, design, write-documentation, and program design or implement if time allows), projecting the terminal and the canvas. Short slide blocks introduce each concept, then the live run applies it. Questions get answered as they come up, mostly while the agent works. There is no in-class práctica and no homework.

Materials (mirrored from the repo branch `feat/session-4-deck`, `e0f75d2`): [[INSTRUCTOR]], [[slides]]. The animated deck (`sessions/session-4/deck/index.html`) lives in the repo only. It is built on Session 2's deck (same palette, mascot, route and kurasu slides API) and carries no live content and no timing.

## The deck (15 slides)

| # | Slide | Content |
|---|---|---|
| 1–3 | Portada, Hoy, ¿Cómo les fue? | Recap: a new skill, what you still had to explain (Session 3's homework), doubts left over |
| 4 | Deuda y rendición cognitiva | The session's frame, plus *"Documentar es pensar antes de construir"* |
| 5 | AGENTS.md como índice | Session 3's handover: a 900-line file vs a 30-line index linking to docs, prototypes and the wiki |
| 6 | Qué va en cada lugar | `AGENTS.md`, `docs/`, wiki. Invariants dropped on purpose |
| 7 | Problema y solución | General, no example: one problem, many solutions; starting from the solution lets the agent pick the average answer |
| 8 | Definir el problema: mapear la realidad | Actors, entities, processes, rules; often a product team's job |
| 9 | Definir la solución | Model, flows, states, components, screens, prototypes, each decision with its reason |
| 10 | Documentos vivos | doc → código → review → reconciliar; review asks "did it do what we agreed?" and "were there changes during implementation?" |
| 11 | Un contexto por trabajo | Subagents: scout, one per repo, one per facet; only the conclusion comes back |
| 12–15 | Costo, cuándo no usar IA, ser dueño, ¿qué aprendimos? | The base-arc closing. Homework, the Session 5 demos and the arc transition are said aloud, not on a slide |

## Live flow

- **El proyecto**: walk kurasu's `app/AGENTS.md` → `docs/README.md` → architecture index → prototypes → `.mahou/wiki`.
- **El problema**: explore + shape on the chat; **the room answers the shape questions**. Scope fixed up front: "chat for the featured session".
- **La solución**: design along slide 9's six items, with a prototype of the chat panel.
- **Documentar**: write-documentation, showing the docs diff.
- **Subagentes**: the explore scouts always; program design or implement if time allows.
- Before class: a full dry run on a separate branch, kept as a fallback; deploy kurasu if a poll is used.

## Key decisions

- **Live over show-and-tell.** A finished run (`preguntas-en-la-card`) was considered and dropped: watching the decisions get made, with the room making them, makes the cognitive-surrender point better than showing results.
- **The deck never names the chat.** Concept slides only; the live run is the example. The multi-user to-do example was dropped along with it.
- **Dropped from the deck**: the invariants, the `PROJECT.md`/feature templates, the interrogation slide, "va / no va", the plan step in the living-docs chain, the brief slide, "lo que viene".
- **Subagents settled here as use, not primitive.** Session 3 teaches the primitive and installs `pi-subagents`; this session shows them working in a real run.
- **Cost has a home again**: slide 12 (money, context, attention), plus the live run's usage if the tool shows it.
- Cognitive debt/surrender frames the session, introduced up front and returned to in the closing. Title stays **Context Engineering**.

## Open items

- **Homework dropped** (2026-11-02), and `exercise/` deleted with it. `COURSE_PROGRAM.md` is aligned on the same branch. Session 5's demo block still runs this session's recap with that homework; its files need aligning.
- Do the dry run and note where it stalls.
- The branch is pushed but has no pull request yet.

**Topics covered**: [[topic-inventory#[Agus] Tier 4: Context Engineering → Session 4|Tier 4: Context Engineering]] (reshaped: documentation-driven instead of spec-driven)

## Related

- [[sessions/session-3/session-3|Session 3]] — teaches subagents and hands over *`AGENTS.md` as an index*; its homework is this session's recap
- [[sessions/session-6/session-6|Session 6]] — the other closing. This session closes the base arc (cost, limits, career, atrophy); Session 6 closes the course
- [[01_Projects/kurasu/index|Kurasu]] — the live run's project

The animated deck (`sessions/session-4/deck/index.html`) lives in the repo only. It is built on Session 2's deck (same palette, mascot, route and kurasu slides API) and carries no live content and no timing.

## The deck (15 slides)

| # | Slide | Content |
|---|---|---|
| 1–3 | Portada, Hoy, ¿Cómo les fue? | Recap: a new skill, what you still had to explain (Session 3's homework), doubts left over |
| 4 | Deuda y rendición cognitiva | The session's frame, plus *"Documentar es pensar antes de construir"* |
| 5 | AGENTS.md como índice | Session 3's handover: a 900-line file vs a 30-line index linking to docs, prototypes and the wiki |
| 6 | Qué va en cada lugar | `AGENTS.md`, `docs/`, wiki. Invariants dropped on purpose |
| 7 | Problema y solución | General, no example: one problem, many solutions; starting from the solution lets the agent pick the average answer |
| 8 | Definir el problema: mapear la realidad | Actors, entities, processes, rules; often a product team's job |
| 9 | Definir la solución | Model, flows, states, components, screens, prototypes, each decision with its reason |
| 10 | Documentos vivos | doc → código → review → reconciliar; review asks "did it do what we agreed?" and "were there changes during implementation?" |
| 11 | Un contexto por trabajo | Subagents: scout, one per repo, one per facet; only the conclusion comes back |
| 12–15 | Costo, cuándo no usar IA, ser dueño, ¿qué aprendimos? | The base-arc closing. Homework, the Session 5 demos and the arc transition are said aloud, not on a slide |

## Live flow

- **El proyecto**: walk kurasu's `app/AGENTS.md` → `docs/README.md` → architecture index → prototypes → `.mahou/wiki`.
- **El problema**: explore + shape on the chat; **the room answers the shape questions**. Scope fixed up front: "chat for the featured session".
- **La solución**: design along slide 9's six items, with a prototype of the chat panel.
- **Documentar**: write-documentation, showing the docs diff.
- **Subagentes**: the explore scouts always; program design or implement if time allows.
- Before class: a full dry run on a separate branch, kept as a fallback; deploy kurasu if a poll is used.

- **Live over show-and-tell.** A finished run (`preguntas-en-la-card`) was considered and dropped: watching the decisions get made, with the room making them, makes the cognitive-surrender point better than showing results.
- **The deck never names the chat.** Concept slides only; the live run is the example. The multi-user to-do example was dropped along with it.
- **Dropped from the deck**: the invariants, the `PROJECT.md`/feature templates, the interrogation slide, "va / no va", the plan step in the living-docs chain, the brief slide, "lo que viene".
- **Subagents settled here as use, not primitive.** Session 3 teaches the primitive and installs `pi-subagents`; this session shows them working in a real run.
- **Cost has a home again**: slide 12 (money, context, attention), plus the live run's usage if the tool shows it.

# Session 6: Open Source Models & Running on CCAD

The model is one replaceable component. Everything from Sessions 2-5 survives the swap.

The session's line: *"Cambiás el modelo editando cinco líneas de JSON, y nada de lo que construiste en cinco sesiones se cae."*

**Owner**: Diego. **Guest**: Ale Silva (CCAD), confirmed, 30 minutes. **Duration: 2 h 30** — the only session besides Session 1 that isn't 2 h. Materials in Spanish.

> 🔴 **TO REVIEW** — `INSTRUCTOR.md` was Claude-generated and Diego has annotated it across several passes, but the file still carries the review marker.

**Topics covered**: [[topic-inventory#[Diego] Tier 6: Open Source Models & HPC → Session 6|Tier 6: Open Source Models & HPC]] · [[topic-inventory#Cross-cutting: Security & Trust (woven throughout)|Security: you become the operator; "local" isn't automatically private]]

Full instructor notes in [[INSTRUCTOR]]; audience-facing materials in [[slides]] and [[exercise/README|exercise]].

## The gateway redesign

The session was rebuilt around a **LiteLLM gateway** with an OpenAI-compatible endpoint in front of CCAD. That single change is what makes the class deliverable:

- **No SSH, no scheduler, no queue, no port forwarding.** Setup is a provider entry in `~/.pi/agent/models.json` and `/model`.
- **[[sessions/session-5/session-5|Session 5]] is no longer a dependency.** The práctica runs on the gateway, so it survives whatever shape Session 5 takes.
- **CCAD accounts stopped being a calendar blocker.** The hands-on authenticates with an API key — one per student, issued by Diego from his own account. Accounts are still recommended weeks ahead because they outlive the course.
- **Cluster mechanics are out of the course.** Login vs. compute node, the scheduler, modules and port forwarding are internals of a multi-user inference service. Only the shared-resource etiquette survives, as one sentence.

The lesson got stronger, not weaker. Pointing a hand-written harness at another model proves the harness is model-agnostic. Pointing **Pi** at another model proves the thing the course actually cares about: the `AGENTS.md`, the skills, plan mode and the review flow all keep working when you swap the model underneath.

## Block breakdown (2 h 30)

| Block | Time |
|---|---|
| Recap & sharing from Session 5 | 5 min |
| **Guest: Ale Silva — CCAD, LiteLLM, vLLM** | **30 min** |
| **Open-weight models (Diego)** | **30 min** |
| Break | 5 min |
| **Hands-on: CCAD gateway (everyone) + Agus's GPU (optional)** | **60 min** |
| Debrief: is it good enough for a serious project? | 5 min |
| Course closing & retrospective | 15 min |

Exactly 150 minutes — **no slack.** The recap is the elastic block; the hands-on and the closing don't move. Both 30-minute blocks need rehearsing against a clock.

Note the ordering: the debrief comes *after* the hands-on on purpose, and "when open source is the right call" folds into the end of it. Judgment discussions land better once students have measured something themselves.

The theory block was rebuilt on Copes's arc (in Spanish), which narrowed the security thread deliberately: what survives is *you become the operator* and *"local" doesn't automatically mean private*.

## Hands-on (60 min)

Two tracks, both the same operation against different endpoints: add a provider, pick the model with `/model`. **Nobody installs a runtime.**

**Step 0 — `models.json`, everyone together (~8 min).** Walked on screen with the room typing along, left projected for the rest of the hour. The file lives in `~/.pi/agent/` — next door to the global `AGENTS.md` they wrote in Session 3. Good callback.

**Track A — the CCAD gateway (everyone, ~32 min).** Export the key → `/model` → give it a multi-step task **in their own repo, with their own `AGENTS.md` and skills** → repeat with the hosted model → note the difference. Two clean sessions, not one with `/model` in the middle. The session's outcome depends on Track A alone, and that gets said out loud.

**Track B — Agus's GPU, in the room (optional, ~20 min).** Agus serves a small model with Ollama; the room connects with one more entry in the same `models.json`. It teaches what serving-it-yourself didn't: it separates *"open models are worse"* from *"this small quantized model is worse"*, and it puts the model three metres away with the data never leaving the room.

The config file ends with **three providers** — the hosted one, CCAD, and Agus's laptop. The session's thesis stops being a claim and becomes three JSON entries.

> 💡 **Track B's concurrency is content, not a risk.** One GPU serving 25 people queues up — which is exactly what Ale explained half an hour earlier about why CCAD runs vLLM. Narrate it live instead of treating it as a failure.

## Cross-session wiring

- **Session 3** → the unexpected payoff: their `AGENTS.md`, skills and config keep working against a model running on a UNC cluster.
- **[[sessions/session-4/session-4|Session 4]]** → the context window comes back as a **server startup parameter**, not a product property. And the other cost model: per hour and per GPU, not per token. **The two closings split**: Session 4 closes the base arc (cost, limits, career, atrophy); this one closes the course.
- **Session 1** → LLM + tool + harness; today we swap the L. The course's closing symmetry.
- **[[sessions/session-5/session-5|Session 5]]** → no longer a dependency. Still worth coordinating: if Session 5 leaves students with a client of their own, the closing extension has an audience.

## Open items

- **Run Track A end to end on a clean machine** before class — the only rehearsal that matters, and now short.
- **Verify the open model emits valid tool calls through LiteLLM.** The single point that could topple both tracks: a model that writes well but can't produce a valid tool call leaves the práctica with nothing to show. Test the chain, not the family.
- Test the exact `baseUrl` (with and without `/v1`); pin `contextWindow` to the server's real value once Ale confirms it.
- **Concurrency**: 25-30 simultaneous requests against the gateway. If rate-limited, practise in two waves.
- Validate the per-student key handout with Ale, and distribute the keys before class.
- Confirm Agus brings the portable GPU, which model he serves, and test `OLLAMA_HOST=0.0.0.0` reachable from another machine plus `OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL` under load.
- Ask Ale for the Qwen with lead time, and **set a cutoff date** — past it, the slides close on one model and the third run leaves the exercise.
- Confirm the room allows the extra 30 minutes.
- ⚠️ **`INSTRUCTOR.md` still says the deck and exercise need writing from scratch.** They were rewritten two commits later — that section, and the matching open question in `COURSE_PROGRAM.md`, are stale.

## Related

- [CCAD](https://supercomputo.unc.edu.ar/ccad/) · [wiki](https://wiki.ccad.unc.edu.ar/) · [opening an account](https://wiki.ccad.unc.edu.ar/empezar/abrir-cuenta.html) · [equipment](https://supercomputo.unc.edu.ar/equipamiento/) · [status](https://stats.ccad.unc.edu.ar/)
- [Raschka — using local coding agents](https://magazine.sebastianraschka.com/p/using-local-coding-agents) — the appendix for students who want to serve a model at home

# Session 6: Open Source Models & Running on CCAD

The model is one replaceable component. Everything from Sessions 2-5 survives the swap.

The session's line: *"Cambiás el modelo editando cinco líneas de JSON, y nada de lo que construiste en cinco sesiones se cae."*

**Owner**: Diego. **Guest**: Ale Silva (CCAD), confirmed, 30 minutes. **Duration: 2 h 30** — the only session besides Session 1 that isn't 2 h. Materials in Spanish.

> 🔴 **TO REVIEW** — `INSTRUCTOR.md` was Claude-generated and Diego has annotated it across several passes, but the file still carries the review marker.

**Topics covered**: [[topic-inventory#[Diego] Tier 6: Open Source Models & HPC → Session 6|Tier 6: Open Source Models & HPC]] · [[topic-inventory#Cross-cutting: Security & Trust (woven throughout)|Security: you become the operator; "local" isn't automatically private]]

Full instructor notes in [[INSTRUCTOR]]; audience-facing materials in [[slides]] and [[exercise/README|exercise]]. The animated deck (`sessions/session-6/deck/index.html`) lives in the repo only.

## The deck

Built by Diego for the open-weight models block (PR #20, 2026-11-11; PR #21, 2026-11-23), in the dark terminal design, with speaker notes as HTML comments. It runs inside the kurasu classroom on the slides API. It covers only Diego's theory block: no CCAD guest block, no práctica, no closing.

- **Theory, from Copes's *Open-weight AI models***, one slide per section in the post's order: what weights are (a layer drawn as a matrix multiplication), architecture vs weights, what open-weight means, open access / open weights / open source, the training recipe, downloading a local model, quantization, what open weights allow (six items: pin the version, data on your machine, pick who runs it, fine-tune, study it, small models as parts), licenses, recent large releases, why labs release large models (five beneficiaries), what open weights don't guarantee, how to use one, ten evaluation checks over two slides, takeaways.
- **Demo slides**: `ollama run qwen3.5:4b` on the laptop; the same model in Pi through an `ollama` provider in `models.json`; Hugging Face, official collections vs community GGUFs pulled with `ollama run hf.co/...`.
- **Caso real: un Qwen adaptado a Pi** — `harness-hub/Qwen3.8-27B-pi-adapted`, a LoRA adapter trained with RL inside Pi. Under Pi, pass@1 goes from 39.2% to 64.7% on SWE-bench Pro (hard 51) and from 39.5% to 55.8% on Terminal-Bench 2.1, per the model card (Clem Delangue's tweet says 29.4% → 62.7%; the notes explain the gap). It ties fine-tuning to Session 5: the harness is one part, and a model can be trained for it.

## The gateway redesign

The session was rebuilt around a **LiteLLM gateway** with an OpenAI-compatible endpoint in front of CCAD. That single change is what makes the class deliverable:

- **No SSH, no scheduler, no queue, no port forwarding.** Setup is a provider entry in `~/.pi/agent/models.json` and `/model`.
- **[[sessions/session-5/session-5|Session 5]] is no longer a dependency.** The práctica runs on the gateway, so it survives whatever shape Session 5 takes.
- **CCAD accounts stopped being a calendar blocker.** The hands-on authenticates with an API key — one per student, issued by Diego from his own account. Accounts are still recommended weeks ahead because they outlive the course.
- **Cluster mechanics are out of the course.** Login vs. compute node, the scheduler, modules and port forwarding are internals of a multi-user inference service. Only the shared-resource etiquette survives, as one sentence.

The lesson got stronger, not weaker. Pointing a hand-written harness at another model proves the harness is model-agnostic. Pointing **Pi** at another model proves the thing the course actually cares about: the `AGENTS.md`, the skills, plan mode and the review flow all keep working when you swap the model underneath.

## Block breakdown (2 h 30)

| Block | Time |
|---|---|
| Recap & sharing from Session 5 | 5 min |
| **Guest: Ale Silva — CCAD, LiteLLM, vLLM** | **30 min** |
| **Open-weight models (Diego)** | **30 min** |
| Break | 5 min |
| **Hands-on: CCAD gateway (everyone) + Agus's GPU (optional)** | **60 min** |
| Debrief: is it good enough for a serious project? | 5 min |
| Course closing & retrospective | 15 min |

Exactly 150 minutes — **no slack.** The recap is the elastic block; the hands-on and the closing don't move. Both 30-minute blocks need rehearsing against a clock.

Note the ordering: the debrief comes *after* the hands-on on purpose, and "when open source is the right call" folds into the end of it. Judgment discussions land better once students have measured something themselves.

The theory block was rebuilt on Copes's arc (in Spanish), which narrowed the security thread deliberately: what survives is *you become the operator* and *"local" doesn't automatically mean private*.

## Hands-on (60 min)

Two tracks, both the same operation against different endpoints: add a provider, pick the model with `/model`. **Nobody installs a runtime.**

**Step 0 — `models.json`, everyone together (~8 min).** Walked on screen with the room typing along, left projected for the rest of the hour. The file lives in `~/.pi/agent/` — next door to the global `AGENTS.md` they wrote in Session 3. Good callback.

**Track A — the CCAD gateway (everyone, ~32 min).** Export the key → `/model` → give it a multi-step task **in their own repo, with their own `AGENTS.md` and skills** → repeat with the hosted model → note the difference. Two clean sessions, not one with `/model` in the middle. The session's outcome depends on Track A alone, and that gets said out loud.

**Track B — Agus's GPU, in the room (optional, ~20 min).** Agus serves a small model with Ollama; the room connects with one more entry in the same `models.json`. It teaches what serving-it-yourself didn't: it separates *"open models are worse"* from *"this small quantized model is worse"*, and it puts the model three metres away with the data never leaving the room.

The config file ends with **three providers** — the hosted one, CCAD, and Agus's laptop. The session's thesis stops being a claim and becomes three JSON entries.

> 💡 **Track B's concurrency is content, not a risk.** One GPU serving 25 people queues up — which is exactly what Ale explained half an hour earlier about why CCAD runs vLLM. Narrate it live instead of treating it as a failure.

- **Session 3** → the unexpected payoff: their `AGENTS.md`, skills and config keep working against a model running on a UNC cluster.
- **[[sessions/session-4/session-4|Session 4]]** → the context window comes back as a **server startup parameter**, not a product property. And the other cost model: per hour and per GPU, not per token. **The two closings split**: Session 4 closes the base arc (cost, limits, career, atrophy); this one closes the course.
- **Session 1** → LLM + tool + harness; today we swap the L. The course's closing symmetry.
- **[[sessions/session-5/session-5|Session 5]]** → no longer a dependency. Still worth coordinating: if Session 5 leaves students with a client of their own, the closing extension has an audience.

## Open items

- **Run Track A end to end on a clean machine** before class — the only rehearsal that matters, and now short.
- **Verify the open model emits valid tool calls through LiteLLM.** The single point that could topple both tracks: a model that writes well but can't produce a valid tool call leaves the práctica with nothing to show. Test the chain, not the family.
- Test the exact `baseUrl` (with and without `/v1`); pin `contextWindow` to the server's real value once Ale confirms it.
- **Concurrency**: 25-30 simultaneous requests against the gateway. If rate-limited, practise in two waves.
- Validate the per-student key handout with Ale, and distribute the keys before class.
- Confirm Agus brings the portable GPU, which model he serves, and test `OLLAMA_HOST=0.0.0.0` reachable from another machine plus `OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL` under load.
- Ask Ale for the Qwen with lead time, and **set a cutoff date** — past it, the slides close on one model and the third run leaves the exercise.
- Confirm the room allows the extra 30 minutes.

# Kurasu (クラス) — virtual class platform

New project built in the context of [[vibe-coding-to-agentic-engineering|the agentic engineering course]]. A virtual class tool that serves two roles: the running example for the course, and the actual tool the course itself runs on.

**Status:** live in production at https://kurasu.asermax.com, with classes 1 and 2 loaded and the professors registered. Built on 2026-10-18/19 with the mahou workflow (explore → shape → design → program design → test design → implement), and recorded as the agentic demo for session 2. Last recorded deploy: 2026-10-26, email validation (PR #17). The work logs of PRs #18 and #19 (both merged 2026-11-02) still list the manual `pnpm deploy` as pending.

## Where it lives

- Code: `app/` inside `~/workspace/filadd/agentic-engineering-famaf-extension-course` (pnpm + turbo monorepo, package name `kurasu`)
- Branch: `main` (first build and visual adjustments through PR #14, then PRs #15, #17, #18, #19)
- Docs: `app/docs/architecture/` (in Spanish: data model, data access, components, login and access, real-time classroom, slides API, poll/session states, web loading and actions, session news by mail, session feedback, invariants) and HTML prototypes in `app/docs/prototipos/`
- Agent wiki: `.mahou/wiki/` (backend architecture rules, API shape, web patterns, lint/test fence)
- Work logs: `.scratch/aula-virtual/` (first build), `.scratch/ajustes-visuales/` (loading states and action feedback) `.scratch/backlog-kurasu/` (session news by mail), `.scratch/email-valido/`, `.scratch/feedback-de-sesion/` and `.scratch/preguntas-en-la-card/`, each with a `status.md`. Since `feedback-de-sesion` the tasks live in Entire trails (#1 and #3), declared in `.mahou/implement.md`

## What it does

- **Students**: register via QR code → email → magic link, pick an animal avatar; home shows the featured session's card (with its questions when the professor turns them on) and lists every session under "Todas las sesiones", the featured one starred; voting, asking and raising hands only work in the featured session; the classroom shows the professor's slides in sync, with polls, questions, raised hands and material in a side panel; responsive for phone and desktop; dark mode
- **Professors**: desktop admin to create and reorder sessions, upload material (an HTML file can be marked as slides and is checked against the slides API), mark one session as featured (Destacada switch; un-featuring closes its polls, lowers hands and turns off its featured questions in one batch), run polls (multiple choice, word cloud, scale, feedback), manage users and the registration code
- **Session news by mail**: enabling a session, uploading material and opening a poll record a pending news entry for the session; the professor sees them in the session's Contenido tab, discards them or picks some and writes an announcement, which the API mails to everyone with access (professor in To, students in Bcc batches of 49), linking to the session on the student home
- **Session feedback**: a feedback poll where students pick 1–5 with emojis plus an optional comment, can change it while open and never see results; the professor sees five bars and a sheet of each student's answer
- **Email validation**: one shared `Email` schema (trim, lowercase, 254 chars, address pattern) in the API and the web forms; suppressed recipients are dropped on the sending subdomain through an Alchemy resource
- **Real time**: one Durable Object per session pushes changes over WebSocket and tracks who is present
- **Slides API**: the web tells the slides HTML which slide and step to show, and relays the professor's position to the students; session 2's deck already runs on it

## Stack

All on Cloudflare, deployed with Alchemy 2 (`pnpm deploy`, stage `prod`):

- API: Worker built on Effect 4, with ports in `packages/core` and adapters in `packages/database` (Drizzle on D1, through a shared repository with batched statements) and `apps/api` (R2, Email Sending, JWT, Durable Objects)
- Web: TanStack Start (SPA) + Router + React Query, React 19, Tailwind 4
- Storage: D1 for data, R2 for material files; secrets through varlock
- Tooling: TypeScript 7 (tsgo), oxlint + oxfmt, vitest, lefthook; API tests run against a local Alchemy stack

## History

- **2026-10-18/19, first build** (`aula-virtual`): 124 product decisions on canvas, system and program design, test design (API, web and launch trees), tasks T1–T26. Manual validation passed all 82 rows, four agentic review rounds, deployed and launch tree verified in prod
- **2026-10-19, visual adjustments** (`ajustes-visuales`): skeletons and an error screen while pages load, optimistic actions with rollback toasts, pending buttons for confirmations, crow branding. Validated by hand and redeployed
- **2026-10-21/22, session news by mail** (`backlog-kurasu`): the first backlog item. Design on canvas, program and test design, tasks T1–T27 implemented by subagents; along the way the D1 stores moved to a shared repository (find, statements and batches, ordering with nulls) and every table got its own NOT NULL id. Agentic review per batch, human review, and manual validation passed all 20 rows; docs and wiki reconciled with what was built
- **2026-10-26, email validation** (`email-valido`, PR #17): triggered by a failed announcement in prod (502 `MailNotSent`). Deployed to prod with smoke checks
- **2026-11-02, session feedback poll** (`feedback-de-sesion`, PR #18): the backlog item, built as a scored poll with a comment instead of free text. Tasks in Entire trail #1; manual validation, review and reconciliation done
- **2026-11-02, questions on the featured card** (`preguntas-en-la-card`, PR #19): the featured session became an explicit mark (migration `0004_featured_session`) with a core `Batch` port; 39 exploration decisions, shape and design on canvas, tasks in Entire trail #3

## Idea backlog

- Professor-only session messages: students send session-related messages to the professor, visually differentiated from questions
- Expand the slides API to support sending state back from the slides, so any interaction done in the slides can be shared with viewers
- Make slide advancement more resilient by serializing mutations (one change at a time)
- When moving back on the slides, land on the last step of the slide instead of the first
- Allow sending emojis on the slides
- Use constants everywhere (no magic strings/numbers)
- Understand the effect code and establish proper backend layers for reusable code

# Kurasu (クラス) — virtual class platform

New project built in the context of [[vibe-coding-to-agentic-engineering|the agentic engineering course]]. A virtual class tool that serves two roles: the running example for the course, and the actual tool the course itself runs on.

**Status:** live in production at https://kurasu.asermax.com, with classes 1 and 2 loaded and the professors registered. Built on 2026-10-18/19 with the mahou workflow (explore → shape → design → program design → test design → implement), and recorded as the agentic demo for session 2. Last recorded deploy: 2026-10-26, email validation (PR #17). The work logs of PRs #18 and #19 (both merged 2026-11-02) still list the manual `pnpm deploy` as pending.

## Where it lives

- Code: `app/` inside `~/workspace/filadd/agentic-engineering-famaf-extension-course` (pnpm + turbo monorepo, package name `kurasu`)
- Branch: `main` (first build and visual adjustments through PR #14, then PRs #15, #17, #18, #19)
- Docs: `app/docs/architecture/` (in Spanish: data model, data access, components, login and access, real-time classroom, slides API, poll/session states, web loading and actions, session news by mail, session feedback, invariants) and HTML prototypes in `app/docs/prototipos/`
- Agent wiki: `.mahou/wiki/` (backend architecture rules, API shape, web patterns, lint/test fence)
- Work logs: `.scratch/aula-virtual/` (first build), `.scratch/ajustes-visuales/` (loading states and action feedback) `.scratch/backlog-kurasu/` (session news by mail), `.scratch/email-valido/`, `.scratch/feedback-de-sesion/` and `.scratch/preguntas-en-la-card/`, each with a `status.md`. Since `feedback-de-sesion` the tasks live in Entire trails (#1 and #3), declared in `.mahou/implement.md`

## What it does

- **Students**: register via QR code → email → magic link, pick an animal avatar; home shows the featured session's card (with its questions when the professor turns them on) and lists every session under "Todas las sesiones", the featured one starred; voting, asking and raising hands only work in the featured session; the classroom shows the professor's slides in sync, with polls, questions, raised hands and material in a side panel; responsive for phone and desktop; dark mode
- **Professors**: desktop admin to create and reorder sessions, upload material (an HTML file can be marked as slides and is checked against the slides API), mark one session as featured (Destacada switch; un-featuring closes its polls, lowers hands and turns off its featured questions in one batch), run polls (multiple choice, word cloud, scale, feedback), manage users and the registration code
- **Session news by mail**: enabling a session, uploading material and opening a poll record a pending news entry for the session; the professor sees them in the session's Contenido tab, discards them or picks some and writes an announcement, which the API mails to everyone with access (professor in To, students in Bcc batches of 49), linking to the session on the student home
- **Session feedback**: a feedback poll where students pick 1–5 with emojis plus an optional comment, can change it while open and never see results; the professor sees five bars and a sheet of each student's answer
- **Email validation**: one shared `Email` schema (trim, lowercase, 254 chars, address pattern) in the API and the web forms; suppressed recipients are dropped on the sending subdomain through an Alchemy resource
- **Real time**: one Durable Object per session pushes changes over WebSocket and tracks who is present
- **Slides API**: the web tells the slides HTML which slide and step to show, and relays the professor's position to the students; session 2's deck already runs on it

## Stack

All on Cloudflare, deployed with Alchemy 2 (`pnpm deploy`, stage `prod`):

- API: Worker built on Effect 4, with ports in `packages/core` and adapters in `packages/database` (Drizzle on D1, through a shared repository with batched statements) and `apps/api` (R2, Email Sending, JWT, Durable Objects)
- Web: TanStack Start (SPA) + Router + React Query, React 19, Tailwind 4
- Storage: D1 for data, R2 for material files; secrets through varlock
- Tooling: TypeScript 7 (tsgo), oxlint + oxfmt, vitest, lefthook; API tests run against a local Alchemy stack

## History

- **2026-10-18/19, first build** (`aula-virtual`): 124 product decisions on canvas, system and program design, test design (API, web and launch trees), tasks T1–T26. Manual validation passed all 82 rows, four agentic review rounds, deployed and launch tree verified in prod
- **2026-10-19, visual adjustments** (`ajustes-visuales`): skeletons and an error screen while pages load, optimistic actions with rollback toasts, pending buttons for confirmations, crow branding. Validated by hand and redeployed
- **2026-10-21/22, session news by mail** (`backlog-kurasu`): the first backlog item. Design on canvas, program and test design, tasks T1–T27 implemented by subagents; along the way the D1 stores moved to a shared repository (find, statements and batches, ordering with nulls) and every table got its own NOT NULL id. Agentic review per batch, human review, and manual validation passed all 20 rows; docs and wiki reconciled with what was built
- **2026-10-26, email validation** (`email-valido`, PR #17): triggered by a failed announcement in prod (502 `MailNotSent`). Deployed to prod with smoke checks
- **2026-11-02, session feedback poll** (`feedback-de-sesion`, PR #18): the backlog item, built as a scored poll with a comment instead of free text. Tasks in Entire trail #1; manual validation, review and reconciliation done
- **2026-11-02, questions on the featured card** (`preguntas-en-la-card`, PR #19): the featured session became an explicit mark (migration `0004_featured_session`) with a core `Batch` port; 39 exploration decisions, shape and design on canvas, tasks in Entire trail #3

## Idea backlog

- Professor-only session messages: students send session-related messages to the professor, visually differentiated from questions
- Expand the slides API to support sending state back from the slides, so any interaction done in the slides can be shared with viewers
- Make slide advancement more resilient by serializing mutations (one change at a time)
- When moving back on the slides, land on the last step of the slide instead of the first
- Allow sending emojis on the slides
- Use constants everywhere (no magic strings/numbers)
- Understand the effect code and establish proper backend layers for reusable code

- **Professors**: desktop admin to create and reorder sessions, upload material (an HTML file can be marked as slides and is checked against the slides API), mark one session as featured (Destacada switch; un-featuring closes its polls, lowers hands and turns off its featured questions in one batch), run polls (multiple choice, word cloud, scale, feedback), manage users and the registration code
- **Session news by mail**: enabling a session, uploading material and opening a poll record a pending news entry for the session; the professor sees them in the session's Contenido tab, discards them or picks some and writes an announcement, which the API mails to everyone with access (professor in To, students in Bcc batches of 49), linking to the session on the student home
- **Session feedback**: a feedback poll where students pick 1–5 with emojis plus an optional comment, can change it while open and never see results; the professor sees five bars and a sheet of each student's answer
- **Email validation**: one shared `Email` schema (trim, lowercase, 254 chars, address pattern) in the API and the web forms; suppressed recipients are dropped on the sending subdomain through an Alchemy resource
- **Real time**: one Durable Object per session pushes changes over WebSocket and tracks who is present
- **Slides API**: the web tells the slides HTML which slide and step to show, and relays the professor's position to the students. The professor's moves are saved one at a time, and moving back lands on the previous slide's last step. The decks of sessions 2, 4 and 6 run on it

## Stack

All on Cloudflare, deployed with Alchemy 2 (`pnpm deploy`, stage `prod`):

- API: Worker built on Effect 4, with ports in `packages/core` and adapters in `packages/database` (Drizzle on D1, through a shared repository with batched statements) and `apps/api` (R2, Email Sending, JWT, Durable Objects)
- Web: TanStack Start (SPA) + Router + React Query, React 19, Tailwind 4
- Storage: D1 for data, R2 for material files; secrets through varlock
- Tooling: TypeScript 7 (tsgo), oxlint + oxfmt, vitest, lefthook; API tests run against a local Alchemy stack

## History

- **2026-10-18/19, first build** (`aula-virtual`): 124 product decisions on canvas, system and program design, test design (API, web and launch trees), tasks T1–T26. Manual validation passed all 82 rows, four agentic review rounds, deployed and launch tree verified in prod
- **2026-10-19, visual adjustments** (`ajustes-visuales`): skeletons and an error screen while pages load, optimistic actions with rollback toasts, pending buttons for confirmations, crow branding. Validated by hand and redeployed
- **2026-10-21/22, session news by mail** (`backlog-kurasu`): the first backlog item. Design on canvas, program and test design, tasks T1–T27 implemented by subagents; along the way the D1 stores moved to a shared repository (find, statements and batches, ordering with nulls) and every table got its own NOT NULL id. Agentic review per batch, human review, and manual validation passed all 20 rows; docs and wiki reconciled with what was built
- **2026-10-26, email validation** (`email-valido`, PR #17): triggered by a failed announcement in prod (502 `MailNotSent`). Deployed to prod with smoke checks
- **2026-11-02, session feedback poll** (`feedback-de-sesion`, PR #18): the backlog item, built as a scored poll with a comment instead of free text. Tasks in Entire trail #1; manual validation, review and reconciliation done
- **2026-11-02, questions on the featured card** (`preguntas-en-la-card`, PR #19): the featured session became an explicit mark (migration `0004_featured_session`) with a core `Batch` port; 39 exploration decisions, shape and design on canvas, tasks in Entire trail #3
- **2026-11-02, slide moves and home skeleton** (`c2aa15c`, `b0f07b0`, `e4a0e9d`, merged into `main` with the Session 4 branch): the professor's slide moves are serialized and moving back keeps the screen on the last step; the featured card shows one fixed-size skeleton until its polls and questions arrive

## Idea backlog

- Professor-only session messages: students send session-related messages to the professor, visually differentiated from questions
- Expand the slides API to support sending state back from the slides, so any interaction done in the slides can be shared with viewers
- Make slide advancement more resilient by serializing mutations (one change at a time)
- When moving back on the slides, land on the last step of the slide instead of the first
- Allow sending emojis on the slides
- Use constants everywhere (no magic strings/numbers)
- Understand the effect code and establish proper backend layers for reusable code

# From Vibe Coding to Agentic Engineering

6-week course for university CS students on the full spectrum of AI-assisted development — from pure vibe coding to structured agentic engineering. FaMAF extension course.

> **Source of truth**: the repo `filadd/agentic-engineering-famaf-extension-course`. Session artifacts here (`INSTRUCTOR.md`, `slides.md`, `exercise/README.md`) are mirrors — edit them in the repo, not here. The `session-N.md` notes are vault-native.
>
> **Mirror state, 2026-11-23.** Every session artifact and [[topic-inventory]] mirror `main` at `f4eb3fe`. Session 4 has no `exercise/` any more. Session 3's `INSTRUCTOR.md` and `slides.md` picked up Diego's Oct 25–26 commits pushed straight to `main` after PR #16 merged. Session 2 also carries `prompts.md`. The Session 1 PDF export, the HTML decks (`sessions/session-{1,2,3,4,6}/deck/index.html`), Session 5's `propuesta-mcp/` deck, Session 2's vibe-coded demo app and its replay (`sessions/session-2/{app,replay}/`) and the `session-replay` skill (`.claude/skills/`) stay in the repo only.
>
> The repo folded the standalone tier notes into `COURSE_PROGRAM.md` and dropped `resources/`, so [[topic-inventory]] now mirrors that file directly.
>
> **Session materials are in Spanish, instructor notes included**, for every session except Session 5's `INSTRUCTOR.md`. Session 1 switched to Spanish in PR #10. These vault `session-N.md` notes stay in English.

## Format

- 6 sessions, 1 per week, in two arcs — **base (1-4)**: *how do I work well with this thing?*, closed by Session 4; **advanced (5-6)**: *what is this made of, and what if I swap its parts?*, closed by Session 6. Same cohort throughout; the split is announced to students in Session 1
- **Session 1 is 3 hours; the rest are 2** — the extra hour buys introductions, the fundamentals block, and the Pi install
- Theory → hands-on → show-and-tell discussion
- Same project across all sessions; must run in the browser. Students bring their own idea — Session 1 now ships `proyecto-de-respaldo` for those who don't
- Tool: **Pi** (`pi.dev`) — decided. Students install it in Session 1
- Class size: ~30 students, quota of 35. Audience widened in PR #10 to advanced CS students *and* junior programmers

## People

- **Agustin Carrasco** — instructor. Owns sessions 2, 4, 5; the Pi intro and demo in Session 1
- **Diego Piloni** — instructor. Owns sessions 1, 3, 6
- **Ale Silva** (CCAD) — guest, Session 6
- Filadd TAs — floor support during hands-on blocks

## Key Thesis

Vibe coding is a great on-ramp, but professional software development demands accountability. The course shows *why* each level of structure matters by letting students experience the failures firsthand before introducing the solutions.

**Core mental model: "Managing a smart intern."**

**Companion idea: responsibility stays with the person.** If it breaks, if a key leaks, if the code is unmaintainable — you are accountable, not the AI. "The agent wrote it" is not an excuse that exists.

## The Spectrum

1. Vibe Coding — prompt-and-accept, no code review
2. AI-Assisted Coding — copilot completions, developer maintains control
3. Directed AI Assistance — experienced use with constraints, specs, review
4. Agentic Coding — orchestrating AI agents on tasks with oversight
5. Agentic Engineering — full discipline: specs, quality gates, multi-agent coordination

## Repo state (synced 2026-11-23)

Repo: `~/workspace/filadd/agentic-engineering-famaf-extension-course`; `origin/main` is at `f4eb3fe`, and the local checkout is on `main`. **Sessions 1–3 had run** as of the 2026-11-02 sync; later runs are not recorded here.

**Every PR is merged.** `feat/session-4-deck` was merged into `main` on 2026-11-02 without a PR (`f57d9e3`), together with three kurasu web commits. The other session-material changes since PR #16 are Diego's Session 3 deck commits on `main` (Oct 25–26) and the Session 6 deck (#20, #21):

Every session has `INSTRUCTOR.md`, `slides.md` and an `exercise/` in the repo, Session 5 included (written 2026-08-30, program Tier 5 filled in the same day). `COURSE_PROGRAM.md` carries the six tiers, and `resources/` is gone again. `PROGRAMA.md` is the two-page Spanish program for the FaMAF extension submission, which lists Marcos Gómez as docente responsable.

# From Vibe Coding to Agentic Engineering

6-week course for university CS students on the full spectrum of AI-assisted development — from pure vibe coding to structured agentic engineering. FaMAF extension course.

> **Source of truth**: the repo `filadd/agentic-engineering-famaf-extension-course`. Session artifacts here (`INSTRUCTOR.md`, `slides.md`, `exercise/README.md`) are mirrors — edit them in the repo, not here. The `session-N.md` notes are vault-native.
>
> **Mirror state, 2026-11-23.** Every session artifact and [[topic-inventory]] mirror `main` at `f4eb3fe`. Session 4 has no `exercise/` any more. Session 3's `INSTRUCTOR.md` and `slides.md` picked up Diego's Oct 25–26 commits pushed straight to `main` after PR #16 merged. Session 2 also carries `prompts.md`. The Session 1 PDF export, the HTML decks (`sessions/session-{1,2,3,4,6}/deck/index.html`), Session 5's `propuesta-mcp/` deck, Session 2's vibe-coded demo app and its replay (`sessions/session-2/{app,replay}/`) and the `session-replay` skill (`.claude/skills/`) stay in the repo only.
>
> The repo folded the standalone tier notes into `COURSE_PROGRAM.md` and dropped `resources/`, so [[topic-inventory]] now mirrors that file directly.

> **Session materials are in Spanish, instructor notes included**, for every session except Session 5's `INSTRUCTOR.md`. Session 1 switched to Spanish in PR #10. These vault `session-N.md` notes stay in English.

## Format

- 6 sessions, 1 per week, in two arcs — **base (1-4)**: *how do I work well with this thing?*, closed by Session 4; **advanced (5-6)**: *what is this made of, and what if I swap its parts?*, closed by Session 6. Same cohort throughout; the split is announced to students in Session 1
- **Session 1 is 3 hours; the rest are 2** — the extra hour buys introductions, the fundamentals block, and the Pi install
- Theory → hands-on → show-and-tell discussion
- Same project across all sessions; must run in the browser. Students bring their own idea — Session 1 now ships `proyecto-de-respaldo` for those who don't
- Tool: **Pi** (`pi.dev`) — decided. Students install it in Session 1
- Class size: ~30 students, quota of 35. Audience widened in PR #10 to advanced CS students *and* junior programmers

## People

- **Agustin Carrasco** — instructor. Owns sessions 2, 4, 5; the Pi intro and demo in Session 1
- **Diego Piloni** — instructor. Owns sessions 1, 3, 6
- **Ale Silva** (CCAD) — guest, Session 6
- Filadd TAs — floor support during hands-on blocks

## Key Thesis

Vibe coding is a great on-ramp, but professional software development demands accountability. The course shows *why* each level of structure matters by letting students experience the failures firsthand before introducing the solutions.

**Core mental model: "Managing a smart intern."**

**Companion idea: responsibility stays with the person.** If it breaks, if a key leaks, if the code is unmaintainable — you are accountable, not the AI. "The agent wrote it" is not an excuse that exists.

## The Spectrum

1. Vibe Coding — prompt-and-accept, no code review
2. AI-Assisted Coding — copilot completions, developer maintains control
3. Directed AI Assistance — experienced use with constraints, specs, review
4. Agentic Coding — orchestrating AI agents on tasks with oversight
5. Agentic Engineering — full discipline: specs, quality gates, multi-agent coordination
