    '     6\t\n' +
    '     7\t# Worker API\n' +
    '     8\t\n' +
    '     9\t## 🔭 Overview\n' +
    '    10\t\n' +
    "    11\tThe Worker's API is the plugin's only way to reach tentacles: seven calls (create, prompt, answer, close, messages, status, list) and one socket per session. Every request and every socket carries the API key, and the plugin reads the Worker's URL and the key from environment variables. The socket sends one construct, the session state, when it connects and again on every change, and the status call returns the same construct. Calls on an existing session succeed, closed ones included; a deleted or unknown session returns an error.\n" +
    '    12\t\n' +
    '    13\t## ♠️ What it exposes\n' +
    '    14\t\n' +
    '    15\t| Member | Takes | Answers | Who asks |\n' +
    '    16\t|---|---|---|---|\n' +
    '    17\t| `create` | the name, the parent, the settings, the first prompt, and optionally a skills archive, an agents archive and a context archive (see below) | starts the session, stores its skills and agent definitions, sets up its workspace from the repository and the skills and context archives, waits until its first run has started and returns its session id; when the setup fails, returns an error naming the cause and leaves the session failed | the spawn tool |\n' +
    '    18\t| `prompt` | the session id, the text, and a mode: follow-up or steer | sends the text to the session; on an idle, failed or closed session it starts a new run, reopening a closed one; a prompt sent while a question waits is a steer whatever its mode, and queues until the answer | the prompt tool |\n' +
    '    19\t| `answer` | the session id, the question id and the answer text | resolves the waiting question, and the run continues | the answer tool |\n' +
    '    20\t| `close` | the session id | aborts whatever the session is doing and closes it | the close tool |\n' +
    '    21\t| `messages` | the session id and a count, 1 when absent | the last entries of the root conversation, as many as the count | the messages tool |\n' +
    "    22\t| `status` | the session id | the session state at any time | the plugin, when it needs one session's state |\n" +
    "    23\t| `list` | the parent | all of the parent's sessions from the registry, closed ones included, each with its id, name, status, settings and the names of its skills and agents | the list tool and the start-up sync |\n" +
    "    24\t| socket | the session id, on connect | the session state on connect and on every change | the helper's watch, one socket per session |\n" +
    '    25\t\n' +
    "    26\tA message is any entry in the root conversation's history: a user prompt, the agent's text, a tool call or its result, a subagent's result. The last N messages are the last N entries, returned unshortened; the calling agent handles their length. `messages` does not read subagent conversations.\n" +
    '    27\t\n' +
    "    28\tThe registry entry carries each session's name, status, settings and skill and agent names, so `list` answers without a call per session.\n" +
    '    29\t\n' +
    '    30\tA call or a socket on a deleted or unknown session, or an answer to a question that is not waiting, returns an error with a message. The plugin hands that message to the parent agent as a tool failure.\n' +
    '    31\t\n' +
    '    32\t## 🚀 What create takes\n' +
    '    33\t\n' +
    '    34\t| Input | What it holds |\n' +
    '    35\t|---|---|\n' +
    '    36\t| name | required; the status line shows the session by it |\n' +
    "    37\t| parent | the parent's harness (pi or claude) and that harness's session id |\n" +
    '    38\t| settings | provider, model, effort, image and size, and optionally a repository: its `https://` (or `http://`) URL and a shallow-or-full clone flag |\n' +
    '    39\t| prompt | the first prompt; the run starts on it |\n' +
    '    40\t| skills | optional; a gzip-compressed tar file of at most 5 MB with one skill folder per top-level entry |\n' +
    '    41\t| agents | optional; a gzip-compressed tar file of at most 5 MB with one agent definition file per top-level entry |\n' +
    '    42\t| context | optional; a gzip-compressed tar file of at most 5 MB with one top-level entry per file or folder the parent sent |\n' +
    '    43\t\n' +
    "    44\tCreate's body is JSON and carries each archive base64-encoded, which makes it a third larger than the file. Three archives at the 5 MB limit come to about 20 MB.\n" +
    '    45\t\n' +
    "    46\tThe plugin fills every unset setting from its defaults, so create always carries provider, model, effort, image and size. A repository is optional; the workspace's setup clones it into `/workspace/repo` (see [workspace](workspace.md)). Its URL is an `https://` (or `http://`) URL, since the workspace adds the GitHub token to HTTPS requests only, and a create with any other form, such as a bare `github.com/owner/name` or `git@github.com:owner/name`, fails the schema check.\n" +
    '    47\t\n' +
    "    48\tThe plugin's helper checks the skills, agent definitions and context paths on the parent's machine and packs the archives only when every check passes, so the problems it finds reach the parent as the spawn tool's result and no create call is sent. [sessions](sessions.md) covers the checks, in its Skills and agents and Context files sections, and what the session does with each archive.\n" +
    '    49\t\n' +
    '    50\tThe session reads each archive again and runs the same checks, reading frontmatter the same way the helper does. When it cannot read one or more archives, create returns one error that names each invalid archive and its problem. That happens when the file is not a gzip-compressed tar, a file in the skills archive sits outside a skill folder, a skill folder has no SKILL.md, a file in the agents archive is not at its top level, or a skill or agent definition breaks a rule. The session then stores nothing and starts no run. It hands the skills archive to the workspace as sent. The context archive is checked only for being readable, and an empty one is accepted; the session hands it to the workspace as sent. A create that does not come through the helper therefore puts every definition in `/workspace/skills` as written, including one the helper would have quoted.\n' +
    '    51\t\n' +
    "    52\tOnce the archives pass, create sets up the session's workspace and answers only when the setup ends. When the setup fails, create returns an error whose message names the cause in plain words: a repository URL that does not exist, a token that cannot read the repository, GitHub not answering, or an archive that cannot be expanded; any other error comes back as it was captured. The session stays, failed, with that error as its failure, and no run starts (see [sessions](sessions.md)).\n" +
    '    53\t\n' +
    '    54\t## 📡 Session state\n' +
    '    55\t\n' +
    "    56\tThe session state carries the session's status (running, waiting, idle, failed or closed), its settings, the names of its skills and agents, the question while one waits, and the failure when the last run failed or the workspace's setup failed. The question holds its id and its text (see [question-round-trip](question-round-trip.md)). When a run just finished, the state also carries the run's last entry, so the finish wake needs no messages call. A session already idle when the socket connects sends its state without the last entry, and the helper fetches it with `messages`. The socket sends the state when it connects and again on every change; status returns it too. [sessions](sessions.md) lists the states and the events that move a session between them.\n" +
    '    57\t\n' +
    '    58\t> [!NOTE] Why the session state is one construct\n' +
    '    59\t> The finish notice, a new question, the status line, a reconnecting parent and the status call all read the same state, so each of them sees the same session, and a parent that was not connected when something changed learns it from the state sent on connect.\n' +
    '    60\t\n' +
    '    61\t---\n' +
    '    62\t\n' +
    '    63\tRelated: [runtime-components](runtime-components.md), [sessions](sessions.md), [question-round-trip](question-round-trip.md), [plugin](plugin.md)'

<result>plugin:
     1	---
     2	title: "Plugin"
     3	summary: "The tentacles plugin for pi and Claude Code: its parts on the developer's machine, the tools the parent agent sees, the wake messages, how the parent's local list of remote sessions stays in sync, and how the plugin is published and installed."
     4	created: "2026-11-09"
     5	---
     6	
     7	# Plugin
     8	
     9	## 🔭 Overview
    10	
    11	The tentacles plugin gives a parent agent on pi or Claude Code one tool per action on its remote sessions: spawn, prompt, messages, wait (pi only), list, close and answer. It is built from one source into a pi package, published to npm, and a Claude plugin, published as a Claude Code marketplace. Each tool call runs a bundled helper CLI that calls the [Worker API](worker-api.md), and a long-running watch holds one socket per open session to update the status line and wake the parent when a session asks, finishes or fails. The plugin keeps a local list of the parent's remote sessions per harness session and syncs it with the Worker when the harness starts. It reaches tentacles only through the Worker API and the session sockets.
    12	
    13	## 🏗️ Architecture
    14	
    15	```mermaid
    16	flowchart LR
    17	    subgraph inputs["Inputs"]
    18	        Env@{ shape: rect, label: "Environment<br/>Worker URL, API key,<br/>setting defaults" }
    19	        Agent@{ shape: stadium, label: "Parent agent<br/>tool calls" }
    20	    end
    21	    subgraph plugin["tentacles plugin (pi package / Claude plugin, one source)"]
    22	        direction LR
    23	        Glue@{ shape: rect, label: "Harness glue<br/>pi extension / Claude mod" }
    24	        Skill@{ shape: hex, label: "Skill<br/>protocol, remote children" }
    25	        Helper@{ shape: rect, label: "Helper CLI<br/>one call per command,<br/>watch: one socket per open session" }
    26	        Local@{ shape: cyl, label: "Local state<br/>pi session entry /<br/>CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA file" }
    27	        Glue -->|"command and arguments"| Helper
    28	        Helper -->|"result or error"| Glue
    29	        Glue -->|"read at start, write on change"| Local
    30	        Helper -->|"state events from watch"| Glue
    31	    end
    32	    Worker@{ shape: cloud, label: "Worker API<br/>and session sockets" }
    33	    Status@{ shape: rect, label: "Status line<br/>name and status per session" }
    34	    Wake@{ shape: rect, label: "Wake message<br/>question or last message" }
    35	    Env --> Glue
    36	    Agent -->|"one tool per action"| Glue
    37	    Helper -->|"API key"| Worker
    38	    Glue --> Status
    39	    Glue --> Wake
    40	    Skill -.->|"teaches the tools"| Agent
    41	
    42	    classDef grey fill:#f3f4f6,stroke:#4b5563,color:#1f2937
    43	    classDef blue fill:#dbeafe,stroke:#2563eb,color:#1f2937
    44	    classDef green fill:#dcfce7,stroke:#16a34a,color:#1f2937
    45	    classDef amber fill:#fef3c7,stroke:#d97706,color:#1f2937
    46	    classDef orange fill:#ffedd5,stroke:#ea580c,color:#1f2937
    47	    classDef violet fill:#ede9fe,stroke:#7c3aed,color:#1f2937
    48	    class Agent grey
    49	    class Env,Status,Wake blue
    50	    class Glue,Helper green
    51	    class Skill amber
    52	    class Local orange
    53	    class Worker violet
    54	```
    55	
    56	The **harness glue** is a pi extension on pi and a Claude mod on Claude Code. It registers the tools, turns each tool call into a helper command, keeps the parent's local state, updates the status line and delivers the wakes.
    57	
    58	The **helper CLI** runs as one process per command, and as a long-running watch that holds one socket per open session in the local state and hands each state change back to the glue. For spawn it also stats the skill, agent and context paths the agent passed, reads only each SKILL.md and agent definition file to check them, checks that the context paths are files or folders with distinct names, and packs one archive per kind with a filesystem packer that reads the files as it packs (see [sessions](sessions.md)). It reads the Worker URL and the API key from environment variables, and the default session settings come from environment variables too (see Implementation details).
    59	
    60	The **local state** is the parent's list of remote sessions, per harness session: a custom session entry on pi, a file under `CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA` on Claude Code. The glue reads it when the harness starts and writes it whenever the parent's sessions change.
    61	
    62	The **skill** teaches the parent agent the tools and adds that its children are remote: nothing of theirs runs locally, and their state and output are reachable only through the tools. It says that a session's skills and agent definitions are fixed at spawn, so the parent includes everything the job needs in the spawn, and spawns a new session when the job needs a different set. It also explains `context`: each path lands at `/workspace/context/<basename>`, outside the repository, as a copy fixed at spawn whose edits stay in the remote session and never come back, so the parent tells the remote agent in the handoff what the files are and how to use them. It tells the parent to write the handoff so the remote agent decides wherever a skill would stop for the user, ignores any instruction to ask the user, and lists those decisions in its final report. It also tells the parent to say in the handoff what to do at the stop points the agent cannot decide, such as a credential it lacks.
    63	
    64	## ♠️ What it exposes
    65	
    66	| Tool | On Claude Code (model sees) | On pi | Worker call |
    67	|---|---|---|---|
    68	| spawn | `mcp__tentacles__spawn` | `tentacles_spawn` | create |
    69	| prompt | `mcp__tentacles__prompt` | `tentacles_prompt` | prompt |
    70	| messages | `mcp__tentacles__messages` | `tentacles_messages` | messages |
    71	| wait | none | `tentacles_wait` | waits on the session socket |
    72	| list | `mcp__tentacles__list` | `tentacles_list` | list |
    73	| close | `mcp__tentacles__close` | `tentacles_close` | close |
    74	| answer | `mcp__tentacles__answer` | `tentacles_answer` | answer |
    75	
    76	Each tool takes the arguments of its Worker API call and returns its result, except where the plugin fills in the parent itself. spawn takes the name, the first prompt, any settings the agent sets, and optionally skill folder paths, agent definition paths and context file or folder paths; the plugin fills every other setting from its defaults (see Implementation details). When a skill, an agent definition or a context path fails a check, spawn returns every problem with its path, in a Skills, an Agents and a Context group, and creates nothing. list takes no arguments. A Worker error, such as a deleted or unknown session or an answer to a question that is not waiting, reaches the agent as a tool failure carrying the Worker's message. When the plugin gets no usable answer from the Worker, the tool fails with an error naming the cause: the Worker did not answer at its URL, it answered with an unexpected status, or a required variable is unset. On Claude Code the plugin registers the tools by their bare names and the model sees them under the plugin's MCP prefix; on pi they carry the `tentacles_` prefix themselves.
    77	
    78	> [!NOTE] Why Claude Code has no wait tool
    79	> The Claude mod runs every helper process with `$.process.run`, which Claude Code caps at ten minutes, so a wait could not block until a remote agent stops. The mod has no need for one either: it wakes the parent itself by submitting the wake as a prompt, which starts a turn once the session is idle.
    80	
    81	## ⏰ Wake messages
    82	
    83	The watch wakes the parent with what it needs to act without another call:
    84	
    85	| When | What the parent receives |
    86	|---|---|
    87	| a remote agent asks a question | the session, the question id and the question text |
    88	| a run finishes | the session and its last message |
    89	| a run fails | the session and its failure |
    90	
    91	[question-round-trip](question-round-trip.md) follows a question to the parent and back.
    92	
    93	On pi, a wake that arrives while the wait tool is waiting becomes the wait's result instead of a message. A wake that arrives while no wait is running goes out as a message, which pi holds until the parent's turn ends; the next wait returns that wake at once, unless the session has started running again since, and the wait after it waits for a new change.
    94	
    95	> [!NOTE] Why the next wait returns a wake that already went out
    96	> A wake can go out as a message while the parent's turn is still running, before the parent calls the wait. Returning it from the next wait keeps that wait from hanging on a change that already happened.
    97	
    98	> [!WARNING] A headless parent gets no wake
    99	> A parent running headless (`claude -p`) is never woken, the same as with local subagents. It learns of a question or a finished run only by calling the tools, and a question it never reads keeps its session waiting.
   100	
   101	## 🔄 Parent state and sync
   102	
   103	```mermaid
   104	sequenceDiagram
   105	    autonumber
   106	    actor A as Parent agent
   107	    participant G as Plugin glue
   108	    participant L as Local list
   109	    participant H as Helper watch
   110	    participant W as Worker and registry
   111	    participant St as Status line
   112	    opt harness starts with a list that is not empty
   113	        G->>W: list
   114	        W-->>G: the parent's sessions, closed included
   115	        G->>L: replace the list
   116	    end
   117	    A->>G: spawn, close, or a prompt that reopens
   118	    G->>L: add, mark closed, or mark open
   119	    H->>G: state event
   120	    G->>L: update the status
   121	    A->>G: a call on a session
   122	    G->>W: the call
   123	    W-->>G: the session does not exist
   124	    G->>L: remove it
   125	    L->>St: open sessions
   126	```
   127	
   128	The plugin keeps, per harness session, the parent's remote sessions with their name and status, closed ones included. The parent is identified by its harness and that harness's session id, which the Worker also stores on each session.
   129	
   130	When the harness starts and the local list is not empty, the plugin asks the Worker for the parent's sessions and replaces the list with the answer (1 to 3). With an empty list, the plugin makes no call. A forked parent (pi's `/fork`, Claude Code's `/branch` or `--fork-session`) has a new session id, so its first sync returns nothing and its list empties: a fork sees none of the original's remote sessions.
   131	
   132	spawn adds a session, close marks it closed, and a prompt that reopens a closed session marks it open again (4, 5). The watch holds a socket for each open session in the list, and every state event updates that session's status (6, 7). A closed session has no socket until a prompt reopens it, which restarts the watch with the session included.
   133	
   134	Closed sessions stay in the list and in the list tool's result, so the parent can reopen one. The status line shows only the open sessions (12); a sync that returns a closed session brings it back as closed, hidden from the status line.
   135	
   136	A deleted session leaves the list the first time the plugin learns of it: the start-up sync omits it (1 to 3), or any call on it (prompt, messages, close or answer) returns that the session does not exist (8 to 11), or, for an open session, the watch's socket reports that the session does not exist.
   137	
   138	> [!NOTE] Why the list is kept both locally and in the Worker
   139	> The local list lets a harness that has never spawned a remote session start without calling the Worker. The Worker's copy lets a harness that does have sessions recover their current status, including changes it missed while it was closed.
   140	
   141	> [!WARNING] A deleted session lingers until the plugin learns of it
   142	> The daily cleanup deletes a session without telling its parent. The local list still names the session, and so does the status line if the session was open. This lasts until the next start-up sync, the next call on the session, or, for an open session, the watch's next connection to it.
   143	
   144	## 📦 Publishing and installing
   145	
   146	The build produces the plugin as two artifacts that ship separately. The pi package goes to npm as `@asermax/pi-tentacles`, and the Claude plugin goes to the repository's `claude-marketplace` branch, which Claude Code reads as a marketplace. Both carry one version, the contents of the `VERSION` file at the repository root. The build reads it through `apps/plugin/build/version.ts`, which rejects a value that is not a semver string, and writes it into the pi package's manifest, into the Claude plugin's `plugin.json` and into the plugin's entry in `marketplace.json`.
   147	
   148	```mermaid

   174	A release is automatic. On a push to `master` that changes a file the plugin is built from, its sources, build and publish scripts, manifest and README, worker-api, whose API definition and schemas the plugin bundles, or the lockfile and the root manifest, semantic-release reads the conventional commits since the last `v*` tag and picks the next version: `fix` makes a patch, `feat` a minor and a breaking change a major, while commits of other types release nothing. qrt:
     1	---
     2	title: "Question round trip"
     3	summary: "How a remote agent's question travels from its question tool to the parent agent, and how the answer resolves the waiting tool call."
     4	created: "2026-11-09"
     5	---
     6	
     7	# Question round trip
     8	
     9	## 🔭 Overview
    10	
    11	A remote agent asks its parent through its question tool, `ask_parent`, which waits inside the run. The session stores the question and moves to waiting, the session socket carries it to the plugin's helper, and the helper wakes the parent with the question itself. The parent answers, by itself or after asking the person behind it, and the answer resolves the waiting tool call so the run continues. Only the root conversation's model can ask, never a codemode script. The question waits as long as the parent takes: the workspace's files live with the session, so nothing the agent left unpushed is lost while it waits.
    12	
    13	## 📩 Flow
    14	
    15	```mermaid
    16	sequenceDiagram
    17	    autonumber
    18	    participant A as Remote agent
    19	    participant T as Question tool
    20	    participant S as Session
    21	    participant H as Plugin helper
    22	    participant P as Parent agent
    23	    actor Pe as Person
    24	    participant W as Worker
    25	    A->>T: asks
    26	    T->>S: store the question, move to waiting
    27	    S->>H: session state with the question
    28	    H->>P: wake with the question
    29	    opt the parent asks the person
    30	        P->>Pe: shows the question
    31	        Pe-->>P: the answer
    32	    end
    33	    P->>W: answer tool, by question id
    34	    W->>S: answer
    35	    S-->>A: the tool returns, the run continues
    36	```
    37	
    38	1. The agent calls the question tool.
    39	
    40	> [!NOTE] Only the root conversation asks
    41	> Subagent conversations inside the session do not get the question tool. A child conversation starts with a copy of its owner's extensions, and the question tool belongs to an extension only the root has. The subagent tool leaves that extension out of every copy. The parent reads only the root conversation, so a question from work it never sees would arrive without context.
    42	
    43	2. The session stores the question, its id and its text, and moves to waiting.
    44	3. The socket sends the session state with the question to the plugin's helper.
    45	4. The helper wakes the parent with the question itself: the session, the question id and the text, so the parent can answer without another call.
    46	5. and 6. The parent answers it itself, or shows it to the person and answers when they reply.
    47	7. and 8. The parent answers with the answer tool, by the question's id, through the Worker.
    48	9. The answer resolves the waiting tool call and the run continues. The socket sends the new state.
    49	
    50	A prompt sent while a question waits is a steer whatever mode the parent sends it with, and reaches the agent after the answer; a prompt neither answers nor cancels the question. A question keeps its id when an eviction makes the tool run again, so an answer sent for it still resolves it. Every eviction cuts the waiting tool call off, and pi-durable counts each cut-off toward its restart limit. The session lifts that limit while the question's call is live, so the question survives any number of evictions. An answer to a question that is not waiting returns an error, which the parent sees as a tool failure.
    51	
    52	> [!WARNING] No socket open when the question arrives
    53	> When the parent's helper is not connected (the harness is closed, or the parent runs headless), nothing wakes the parent. The question keeps waiting in the session and arrives with the state on the next connection; until then the run stays waiting and the session is never deleted.
    54	
    55	---
    56	
    57	Related: [sessions](sessions.md), [worker-api](worker-api.md), [workspace](workspace.md), [plugin](plugin.md), [remote-agents](../product-design/remote-agents.md)

pd:
     1	---
     2	title: "Remote agents"
     3	summary: "What it is like for a parent agent, and the person behind it, to dispatch coding agents that run on Cloudflare and follow them through tentacles."
     4	created: "2026-11-09"
     5	---
     6	
     7	# Remote agents
     8	
     9	## 🔭 Overview
    10	
    11	tentacles lets an agent on pi or Claude Code start coding agents that run remotely, on Cloudflare, and work with them the way it works with local subagents: spawn them, prompt and steer them, see when they stop, answer their questions and close them. The parent agent does all of it through a set of tools; nothing of a remote agent runs on the developer's machine. When the parent goes away, a remote agent keeps working and waits on its questions, and the parent finds it when it comes back. Its work stays in its workspace for as long as the remote agent exists: what it pushes survives the remote agent's deletion, and what it does not push goes with the remote agent a month after its last run. Every commit a remote agent makes is authored by the name and email the deploy sets, whoever spawned the agent.
    12	
    13	## 🚀 Spawning a remote agent
    14	
    15	The parent spawns a remote agent with a name, a first prompt and its settings: the provider, the model, the effort level, the container image and size, and optionally a repository to work on. The name is required; the status line and the list show the remote agent by its name. Any setting the parent leaves out takes the plugin's default, which the person can change through environment variables. Spawn answers once the remote agent's workspace is set up, with the repository cloned and its skills and context in place, and the agent then starts working on the first prompt. When the setup fails, spawn returns the reason, such as a repository URL that does not exist or a token that cannot read the repository, and spawn leaves the remote agent failed with that reason; it never starts working.
    16	
    17	With a repository in its settings, the remote agent starts with it cloned. Without one, it clones whatever its prompt names. Claude models run on the person's own Claude subscription, and models from other providers are available too.
    18	
    19	[workspace](../technical-design/workspace.md) covers the workspace's setup, its tools and what survives a container stop.
    20	
    21	The parent can also give the remote agent skills and agent definitions, by passing their folder and file paths at spawn. They are fixed for the remote agent's life, so the parent includes every one the job needs, and work that needs a different set goes to a new remote agent. The plugin checks every skill and agent definition on the developer's machine before anything is sent; when one fails, spawn returns every problem with its path, skills, agents and context listed apart, and no remote agent starts.
    22	
    23	The parent can also send context files, the files and folders on its machine that the repository does not hold, such as a change's scratch files, by passing their paths at spawn. The remote agent finds each one in `/workspace/context` under its own name, outside the repository. The copy is fixed at spawn: the remote agent can change it, but its changes stay in its workspace and never come back to the parent, so work that needs different files goes to a new remote agent. The remote agent is told only that the parent sent files and that they are in `/workspace/context`, so the parent says in its handoff what the files are and how to use them. Two paths with the same name, a path that does not exist, or files that pack over 5 MB fail the spawn in the Context group. [sessions](../technical-design/sessions.md) covers how the context reaches the remote agent.
    24	
    25	## 💬 Prompting and steering
    26	
    27	While a remote agent works, the parent can send it a prompt as a follow-up, which the agent takes up after its current turn, or as a steer, which redirects it mid-run. A prompt to an agent that has finished starts it working again.
    28	
    29	Nobody watches a remote agent live. The parent reads what it did through the messages tool: its last message by default, or the last N, where a message is any entry of its conversation (prompts, its text, tool calls and results, subagent results). On pi, the parent can also block on a remote agent with the wait tool.
    30	
    31	A prompt can name one of the remote agent's skills, as `/skill:<name>` or `/<name>` standing on its own, with a space or the start or end of the prompt on each side. The remote agent receives a short block in its place that points at the skill's instructions, and reads the instructions before acting on the skill. A name the remote agent does not hold, or one inside a path or with punctuation attached, stays as written.
    32	
    33	## 📊 The status line
    34	
    35	The harness shows a status line with the name and status of each open remote agent: running, waiting on a question, idle or failed. The status line hides closed ones, but the list tool still returns them.
    36	
    37	The list belongs to the parent's harness session. When the harness reopens that session, the plugin refreshes the list from tentacles, so the status line shows each agent's current status, including changes made while the parent was away. A forked parent starts with no remote agents of its own.
    38	
    39	The list also returns each remote agent's settings and the names of its skills and agents, so a parent that comes back later knows what each remote agent can do.
    40	
    41	## ⏰ Finish and failure wakes
    42	
    43	When a remote agent's run finishes, the plugin wakes the parent with that agent's last message, so the parent can read the result without another call. When a run fails on an error the agent cannot recover from, the plugin wakes the parent with the failure. In both cases the remote agent stays available: a prompt starts it on a new run.
    44	
    45	> [!WARNING] A headless parent is never woken
    46	> A parent running headless (`claude -p`) gets no wake, as with local subagents. It learns that a remote agent finished or asked something only by calling the tools.
    47	
    48	## 🧩 Skills and agents inside a remote agent
    49	
    50	A remote agent sees its skills and agent definitions by name and description, and loads a skill when a task matches it, reading its instructions and the files they point to. It installs whatever a skill needs to run in its workspace. It can start subagents from its agent definitions by name, and those subagents can start subagents of their own, which cannot start any. A remote agent running a skill works on its own. Where a skill would stop to ask the person, the parent's handoff tells it to decide and report what it decided at the end. For a stop point it cannot decide, such as a missing credential, the handoff says what to do, which can be asking the parent with the question tool. The plugin's skill teaches the parent to write that handoff. [sessions](../technical-design/sessions.md) covers how the skills and agents reach the remote agent.
    51	
    52	## ❓ Questions
    53	
    54	A remote agent can ask its parent a question when it needs a decision. The question can wait any length of time: the remote agent's work stays in its workspace while it waits.
    55	
    56	The plugin wakes the parent with the question itself. The parent can answer on its own or show the question to the person and answer when they reply, which can be much later. The parent answers with the answer tool, and the remote agent continues from where it asked. A prompt sent while a question waits does not answer the question; the prompt reaches the agent after the answer.
    57	
    58	Only the remote agent itself asks; subagents it starts inside its session cannot. [question-round-trip](../technical-design/question-round-trip.md) follows a question from the tool to the parent and back.
    59	
    60	## 🛑 Closing and reopening
    61	
    62	Closing a remote agent stops whatever it is doing. A closed agent leaves the status line but stays in the list, and its messages and status stay readable. A prompt to a closed agent reopens it and starts it working again.
    63	
    64	## 🗑️ Deleted remote agents
    65	
    66	tentacles deletes a remote agent a month after its last run stopped, whether it finished, failed or was closed. Reading its messages or status does not extend the month, and an agent that is working or waiting on a question is never deleted. Branches it pushed stay on GitHub; work it never pushed is deleted with it.
    67	
    68	tentacles does not tell the parent. The remote agent leaves the parent's list the first time the plugin notices: when the harness reopens the session, or when a call on the agent returns that the agent does not exist. Until then it can still appear in the list and the status line.
    69	
    70	## 🖼️ A preview for validation
    71	
    72	A remote agent can check the app it starts in a browser by opening a preview of it: a URL to its port on the preview domain, which carries a random token, together with a browser it drives with agent-browser. It opens the preview, checks what it built and closes it. An agent has one preview at a time; opening another replaces the open one. Other checks, such as calling an API, happen inside the agent's workspace with no preview. The preview closes when the agent's run stops, so it is the agent's way to check its own work, not something the parent or the person browses later. The remote agent has no browser for any other page.
    73	
    74	---
    75	
    76	Related: [plugin](../technical-design/plugin.md), [sessions](../technical-design/sessions.md), [question-round-trip](../technical-design/question-round-trip.md), [workspace](../technical-design/workspace.md), [worker-api](../technical-design/worker-api.md)

  post: ' Pi Durable | Earendil MENU Purpose Values Join Us Posts RFC Pi Radius Lefos Works Pi Durable Date: Thu, 01 Oct 2026 From: Earendil Engineering &lt; rfc@earendil.com &gt; To: You Subject: Pi Durable Today Earendil and the Pi community shipped Pi 1.0 . This reflects our belief that after countless hours of hardening, maintenance, and active development, Pi is now a solid foundation on which to build. Pi also continues to evolve. Together with Pi 1.0, we are shipping an experimental new package called Pi Durable. Pi Durable was built specifically for long-running, durable, and malleable agents that can run anywhere. We would like you to join in the fun and help us make it the best durable harness there is. Why Pi Durable? Pi the coding agent is built to run on your (remote) machine, inside a terminal, driven by one person. If the process dies, you look at what happened and tell it to continue. That is what Pi 1.0 focuses on and excels at, and that is not changing. At Earendil, we want to bring this technology to everyone, in whatever form fits their needs best. For that, we need a harness that runs anywhere, can be reached from different surfaces, supports infinitely long conversations, survives catastrophic internal and external failures, and lets multiple humans steer the same agents. Pi Durable is that harness. It does not replace the Pi coding agent. It is a framework for building any agentic application, coding agents included. It shares not only code with the Pi coding agent, like pi-ai, but also its principles: minimalism and malleability. It also lets us explore designs in this space without disrupting Pi the coding agent. Lessons we learn building agentic applications on Pi Durable will flow back into Pi the coding agent as they prove themselves valuable. What is a harness? Everybody has their own definition of a harness. We wrote about this previously , but let us reintroduce the concept of the harness for Pi Durable. A harness is storage plus the machinery needed to run one or more conversations with large language models in parallel. It provides the tools those models call, and the execution environments the tools run in. A conversation is an interaction between you and an agent, recorded as a transcript. The agent is the large language model together with its settings, like the thinking level, and the tools it can call. Tools do their work through an execution environment, which can be your laptop, a remote VM, or an in-memory sandbox. Which tools and which execution environment an agent gets is up to each conversation. Everything the harness runs, from calling the model to executing a tool, is a task. Like everything in Pi, Pi Durable is built so your agent can understand it. The entire source code, without tests, is about 15,000 lines, which comes out to about 150,000 tokens with GPT and about 250,000 with Claude. That\'s the worst case. To build on Pi Durable, your agent rarely needs all of it; the storage backends alone are 3,000 lines it can usually skip. Now let us give you a little tour of Pi Durable, to illustrate what we built and why we built it. Long runs anywhere We want agents to run for a long time and to be able to run anywhere, where anywhere currently means anywhere there is a JavaScript runtime. In Pi Durable, a harness opens over a storage backend. Pi Durable ships memory, SQLite, and JSONL storage, plus a conformance suite and benchmarks for your own backend. The SQLite and JSONL storage code uses no Node APIs, so with a small adapter it runs on Bun or inside a Cloudflare Durable Object. The storage interface is small and easy to implement on top of whatever you have, like a key-value store or Postgres. One process owns a storage at a time, and other clients attach to that process. On SQLite, the harness only keeps the working set in memory: the active transcripts, live tasks, and pending submissions. Everything else stays on disk until it is needed. Active transcripts are naturally bounded by the model\'s context window, because compaction summarizes older messages before they overflow it. So even a conversation with tens of thousands of messages fits snugly into memory. Tools that need files or a shell get them from an execution environment. Pi Durable ships a Node execution environment, which gives tools access to your local files. Like storage, the execution environment interface is small and easy to implement, so you can also expose remote execution environments to your tools. That allows the harness to run on one machine while its tools run on another. Your env function builds the environment for every tool call, from the conversation\'s working directory, so each conversation can run in a different place. import { BACKGROUND_CONTEXT } from "@earendil-works/chord/context" ; import { createModels } from "@earendil-works/pi-ai/models" ; import { openaiProvider } from "@earendil-works/pi-ai/providers/openai" ; import { createRegistry, Harness } from "@earendil-works/pi-durable" ; import { NodeExecutionEnv } from "@earendil-works/pi-durable/env/node" ; import { openNodeSqliteStorage, } from "@earendil-works/pi-durable/storage/sqlite/node" ; import { CodingTools } from "@earendil-works/pi-durable/tools" ; const context = BACKGROUND_CONTEXT; // every call takes a context for cancellation const models = createModels(); models.setProvider(openaiProvider()); const registry = createRegistry(); registry.install(CodingTools); // read, write, edit, bash const env = ({ cwd }: { cwd?: string }) =&gt; new NodeExecutionEnv({ cwd: cwd ?? process.cwd() }); const harness = await Harness.open( await openNodeSqliteStorage( "./agent.sqlite" ), { models, registry, env }, context, ); // The root conversation: created on first use, and the same one after every // restart. const root = await harness.root(context, { agent: { model: { provider: "openai" , modelId: "gpt-6.1-sol" }, cwd: "/work/repo" , }, }); Survives crashes We want an agent to survive its process dying, whether the laptop sleeps, the container is redeployed, or the machine runs out of memory, and to pick up where it left off. In Pi Durable, every step of a run is a task that stores a checkpoint before it moves on. If the process dies, a new process opens the same storage, finds the unfinished tasks, and continues each one from its last checkpoint. A model request that was cut off is sent again; the partial answer stays in the transcript, marked as aborted. A tool call that was cut off reruns if it is safe to; otherwise the model is told it was interrupted. Pi Durable has no built-in subagents, but they take a few lines of code to build, as the triage tool below shows. A subagent runs in a conversation of its own, so it continues from where it left off too, and a subagent tool that is safe to rerun finds its subagent again and waits for its answer. Queued messages are still queued. A requestId makes a submission exactly-once, so a client that retries after a crash gets the original submission back instead of asking twice. const job = { type : "input" , content: "Fix the flaky login test" , requestId: "job-42" , } as const ; await root.submit(job, context); // The process dies here, in the middle of a tool call. // A new process opens the same storage. const harness = await Harness.open( await openNodeSqliteStorage( "./agent.sqlite" ), { models, registry, env }, context, ); harness.resume(); // continue the interrupted run const root = await harness.root(context); // the same submission, answered const settled = await ( await root.submit(job, context)).wait(context); Many conversations at once We want one harness to run many conversations at the same time, without one blocking another. In Pi Durable, one harness runs as many conversations as you need, concurrently, all with the same guarantees. A conversation starts fresh or forks another one at any point in its transcript, and sees the parent\'s history up to that point without copying it. Think of a Slack channel where your agent answers mentions from anyone. Then somebody opens a thread. The channel can be one conversation, and the thread a fork of it at the message the thread replies to. Both run at the same time and neither blocks the other. const channel = await harness.root(context); const question = await channel.submit( { type : "input" , content: "@agent why did the deploy fail?" }, context, ); const answered = await question.wait(context); // Someone replies to the agent\'s answer in a thread. Every conversation names // its owner, which decides what an abort reaches (more on that under Tasks). // The thread has none. const thread = await channel.fork( answered.answer!, { ownership: { kind: "ownerless" } }, context, ); // Both conversations work at the same time. const inThread = await thread.submit( { type : "input" , content: "@agent can we roll it back?" }, context, ); const inChannel = await channel.submit( { type : "input" , content: "@agent who is on call today?" }, context, ); await Promise.all([inThread.wait(context), inChannel.wait(context)]); Each conversation also stores its own agent: the model, the thinking level, the selected extensions and which of their tools are active, extra instructions, and the working directory in its execution environment. A reviewer next to the main agent can use a cheaper model, read-only tools, and its own checkout. Extensions We want everything an agent can do to be pluggable, and every plugged-in piece to take part in durability. In Pi Durable, an extension is a named bundle of system prompt sections, tools, hooks, and tasks. The application installs extensions in a registry. Each conversation selects which extensions and tools it uses, and stores only their names. System prompt sections The system prompt is rebuilt from the sections of the conversation\'s extensions before every request, so a changed section is picked up by the next request. Pi Durable records what changed in the transcript, at the position where it changed, so a restart or a fork sees exactly what the model saw. On models that support system prompt and tool changes in the middle of a conversation, only the change is sent, so the prompt cache stays valid. import { defineExtension, section } from "@earendil-works/pi-durable" ; const ProjectContext = defineExtension({ name: "project-context" , sections: [ // Read from the conversation\'s execution environment. The files can be // loaded and watched in the background; every request renders the // latest state. section( "agents_md" , (input) =&gt; agentsMd.latest(input.env)), section( "skills" , (input) =&gt; skills.latest(input.env)), ], }); Tools Every tool call runs as its own durable task, and its intent is stored before it runs. After a crash, a tool reruns only if it says that is safe. Otherwise the model is told the call was interrupted, with the output stored so far, and decides what to do. Each conversation can also get its own set of tools, like the Slack thread from earlier, which may search but not deploy. import { Type } from "@earendil-works/pi-ai" ; import { defineTool } from "@earendil-works/pi-durable" ; const searchIssues = defineTool({ name: "search_issues" , description: "Search the issue tracker" , parameters: Type.Object({ query: Type.String() }), replay: "safe" , // only reads, so a rerun after a crash is fine execute: async (args, api) =&gt; { // streamed to every client watching api.output( `searching for ${ args.query }\\n` ); return { content: [{ type : "text" , text: await tracker.search(args.query) }], }; }, }); const deploy = defineTool({ name: "deploy" , description: "Deploy a version to production" , parameters: Type.Object({ version: Type.String() }), // No replay: a deploy interrupted by a crash is reported to the model, // never repeated. execute: async (args) =&gt; ({ content: [{ type : "text" , text: await ci.deploy(args.version) }], }), }); registry.install(defineExtension({ name: "ops" , tools: [searchIssues, deploy] })); // The thread may search, but not deploy. await thread.configure({ tools: { remove: [deploy] } }, context); A tool gets the harness API for its call: it can commit entries and documents, start tasks and conversations, and talk to other conversations. That makes a subagent a few lines of code. A tool creates a conversation it owns, gives it a smaller model and its own instructions, and waits for its answer. The subagent is a conversation like any other, so it survives a crash, counts its own cost, and a UI can show it under the call. import type { AssistantMessage } from "@earendil-works/pi-ai" ; import { AssistantEntry, configure } from "@earendil-works/pi-durable" ; const triage = defineTool({ name: "triage" , description: "Label an incoming issue as bug, feature, or question" , parameters: Type.Object({ issue: Type.String() }), // a rerun after a crash finds the same subagent and the same submission replay: "safe" , execute: async (args, api, context) =&gt; { const child = await api.commit( async (tx) =&gt; { const existing = ( await tx.scanConversations({ ownerTaskId: api.taskId }, 1 ) ).items[ 0 ]; if (existing !== undefined ) return existing.id; // Owned by this call, so aborting the call aborts the subagent. const created = await tx.createConversation({ ownership: { kind: "task" , taskId: api.taskId }, }); // It starts as a copy of this conversation\'s agent. Make it a small // model without tools. await configure(tx, created.id, { model: { provider: "openai" , modelId: "gpt-6-luna" }, tools: [], instructions: "Answer with one word: bug, feature, or question." , }); return created.id; }, context); // lets a UI show the subagent under the call await api.details({ conversationId: child }, context); const subagent = await api.conversation(child, context); const request = { type : "input" , content: args.issue, requestId: `triage:${ api.taskId }` , } as const ; const settled = await ( await subagent!.submit(request, context) ).wait(context); // The answer is an entry in the subagent\'s transc'
}</result>

     7	# Workspace
     8	
     9	## 🔭 Overview
    10	
    11	Each session has one workspace, which the session object creates at spawn through the `Workspace` contract. The provider sets it up before the session's first run: it clones the session's repository into `/workspace/repo` and writes the skills and context the parent sent into `/workspace/skills` and `/workspace/context`. It hands back the tools the agent works with, and each environment defines its own. The workspace's files live with the session: a container that stops keeps them, and deleting the session deletes them. The agent gets a browser only to validate a preview of the app it started.
    12	
    13	## 📜 The workspace contract
    14	
    15	The contract has two members that core calls, `create` and `forward`, and the tools `create` returns, whose `execute` only the harness calls. Nothing else about the environment crosses it: no execution environment, no start, stop or keepalive, no egress setting.

     7	# Cloudflare workspace
     8	
     9	## 🔭 Overview
    10	
    11	On Cloudflare, a session's workspace is a Cloudflare Computer workspace that lives in the session's Durable Object. Its files sit in the object's SQLite and are mounted into the container at `/workspace`, at the same paths on both sides. The agent gets Computer's tools: file tools that work on the object's files directly, and `exec`, which runs a command on the isolate shell or the container. One git client per workspace, with a fetch that adds the GitHub token, serves clone, fetch and push from the object, the shell and codemode; git run inside the container reaches GitHub through the egress gateway, which adds the token there. Computer and the platform run the container's lifecycle: it starts on the first command sent to it and stops when idle.
    12	
    13	## 🖥️ The backends and what each can run
    14	
    15	[Workspace](../../workspace.md) draws how a tool call reaches the files and the backends.
    16	
    17	The workspace registers two backends, and `exec`'s `backend` parameter names one of them on each call:
    18	
    19	| Backend | What it is | What it can run | Output |
    20	|---|---|---|---|
    21	| shell | just-bash in a Dynamic Worker, on the Durable Object's files | text tools such as grep, sed, sort and tar, and `git`, which forwards to the workspace git client; no node, npm or other binaries | the whole output when the command ends |
    22	| container | a Cloudflare container running computerd, with the Durable Object's files mounted at `/workspace` | anything the image holds or the agent installs: node, npm, mise, real git, servers for a preview | each line as it is printed, from Computer's exec event stream |
    23	
    24	The file tools, `read`, `ls`, `find`, `grep`, `write`, `edit` and `delete`, take no backend and work on the Durable Object's files. The provider sets `read`, `ls`, `find` and `grep` to replay safe and `write`, `edit`, `delete` and `exec` to unsafe.
    25	
    26	The provider writes each backend's description, which Computer puts in front of its own text, so the agent picks a backend from what the real setup can do. Where Computer's built-in text does not match the setup, such as the shell's "no direct network", the provider's description corrects it. The provider leaves long commands on the shell, and their output comes back when they end.
    27	
    28	`exec` hands the harness each stdout and stderr event in the order it arrives, then the result with the command, the exit code and the full output. Computer reports a non-zero exit as a success, so the provider sets the error flag itself when the exit code is not 0.
    29	
    30	> [!NOTE] Why the shell's output arrives only at the end
    31	> Computer's shell backend awaits just-bash's `exec` to completion and builds its event stream from the finished result, and just-bash has no output callback. A container command streams; a shell command cannot.
    32	
    33	## 📂 `/workspace` in the Durable Object
    34	
    35	The workspace's files live in the session Durable Object's SQLite, next to pi-durable's tables. computerd mounts them in the container at `/workspace` through FUSE, so `/workspace/repo`, `/workspace/skills` and `/workspace/context` have the same paths for the file tools, the shell and the container. Only `/workspace` is shared: anything the container writes elsewhere sits on the container's own disk and is lost when the container stops. The runtimes mise installs live outside `/workspace`, so the agent installs them again after a stop.
    36	
    37	`node_modules` and every other tree an install writes under `/workspace` sync into the Durable Object like any other file, and the agent's instructions do not mention it.
    38	
    39	> [!NOTE] Why `node_modules` stays in the synced workspace
    40	> Keeping it on the container's disk would hide it from the file tools and the shell, and a stop would lose it. Syncing costs install time instead: an npm install took 11.4 s synced against 4.8 s on the container's disk.
    41	
    42	At spawn, the provider builds the workspace and runs the setup without starting a container: it clones the repository into `/workspace/repo` through the git client and writes the skills and context archives' files into `/workspace/skills` and `/workspace/context` through the workspace's file system. Deleting the session clears the Durable Object's storage, and the workspace's files with it.
    43	
    44	## 🔀 Git and egress

Git run in the isolate shell (2) forwards to the same client (3), whose fetch adds the GitHub token (4); codemode scripts' git goes through the same client. egistry generates the token, records it and the port on the session's entry, replacing any preview already open, and returns the token. When a run stops, the session tells the registry, which clears the session's preview.
    70	
    71	### 🧠 Session Durable Object
    72	
    73	Each session is one Durable Object keyed by its session id, and it fills five roles: `SessionHost`, `SessionStorage` (its SQLite), `WakeTimer` (its alarm), `ParentChannel` (its WebSockets) and `Workspace`. It runs pi-durable's Harness over its SQLite, with the question tool and the `onWake` alarm that resumes a run after an eviction. At spawn it builds the session's Computer workspace in the same SQLite storage and runs its setup; from then on the workspace's files, its git client and its container live in the object ([computer-workspace](computer-workspace.md)). The egress gateway that handles the container's outbound requests, including the CDP relay, also runs in the object. It sends each model call where the session's settings say: Claude models to the shared Claude container, other providers to AI Gateway through `env.AI`. It opens and closes the preview's Browser Run browser through its own binding. The daily cleanup job deletes a session through its Durable Object, which clears the object's storage, the workspace's files included, then removes the session's registry entry itself.
    74	
    75	### 🤖 Shared Claude container
    76	
    77	One container runs pi-claude-code's relay and the claude CLI for every session, on the owner's Claude subscription. No session owns it: a model call from any session keeps it up, and it stops 15 minutes after the last call from any session.
    78	
    79	> [!NOTE] Why the Claude container stops after 15 minutes
    80	> Fifteen minutes outlasts Anthropic's five-minute prompt cache and the time a container takes to start, so a parent that prompts a session again soon after a run finishes reaches a container that is still up and a cache that is still warm.
    81	
    82	### 🧪 Codemode sandbox
    83	
    84	The scripts the agent writes with its codemode tool run in pi-durable's QuickJS sandbox, in a sandbox Durable Object of a separate Worker, which the Worker binds by name. Each session's scripts reach it from the session object, through the `CodeSandbox` contract, and call the workspace's tools by name.
    85	
    86	### 🔐 Credentials and outbound handlers
    87	
    88	No container holds a credential. The Claude container's outbound handler adds the Claude subscription token to every request to Anthropic. The workspace adds the GitHub token in two places outside the container: its git client's fetch, for clone, fetch and push from the session object and the isolate shell, and its egress gateway, for every request the container sends to github.com ([computer-workspace](computer-workspace.md)). Both tokens are Worker secrets, as is the API key and the secret that signs CDP tokens. The author name and email every session commits with are deploy variables; they are not credentials, and [workspace](../../workspace.md) covers how they reach every git route.
    89	
    90	> [!WARNING] Containers run where Cloudflare places them
    91	> Containers are meant to run in North America (regions ENAM and WNAM), and nothing enforces it: Cloudflare offers no region setting for containers a Durable Object owns. A session started far from North America can get a container placed elsewhere, and nothing reports it.
    92	
    93	## 🔌 Which part fills each contract
    94	
    95	| Contract | On Cloudflare |
    96	|---|---|
    97	| `SessionHost` | the session Durable Object, reached by its id |
    98	| `SessionStorage` | the session Durable Object's SQLite |
    99	| `WakeTimer` | the session Durable Object's alarm |
   100	| `ParentChannel` | the session Durable Object's WebSockets |
   101	| `RegistryStore` | the registry Durable Object |
   102	| `Workspace` | a Computer workspace in the session Durable Object, with the isolate shell and container backends ([computer-workspace](computer-workspace.md)) |
   103	| `Browser` | Browser Run through the session object's binding; agent-browser reaches it through the CDP relay in the egress gateway ([preview-and-browser](preview-and-browser.md)) |
   104	| `PreviewRouter` | the token subdomain `https://<token>-tentacles-preview.asermax.com`, served by the Worker's preview route and the registry |
   105	| `ModelProviders` | the shared Claude container for Claude, AI Gateway through `env.AI` for the rest |
   106	| `Scheduler` | a cron trigger on the Worker |
   107	| `CodeSandbox` | a Durable Object in the Codemode Worker |
   108	
   109	## 📦 The deploy stack
   110	
   111	The provider is the `provider-cloudflare` package. It exports an Alchemy stack, which a deploy runs on the stage `prod`. The stack declares the Worker with its routes and cron trigger, the two Durable Object classes, the workspace container's image and the Claude container, the Codemode Worker, the Browser Run and AI bindings, and the secrets and deploy variables. The code that runs in those resources builds the Layer of the contracts from the same declarations ([runtime-components](../../runtime-components.md)).

A tool with the same name in a later extension replaces the earlier one, for example a bash that runs inside a Python virtualenv. A wrap decorates whichever tool won, wherever the wrapping extension is selected. import { wrapTool } from "@earendil-works/pi-durable" ; import { createBashTool } from "@earendil-works/pi-durable/tools" ; // Times every bash call, whichever bash the conversation ends up with. const Timing = defineExtension({ name: "timing" , wraps: [ wrapTool(createBashTool(), (bash) =&gt; ({ ...bash, execute: async (args, api, context) =&gt; { const start = Date.now(); try { return await bash.execute(args, api, context); } finally { metrics.record( "bash" , Date.now() - start); } }, })), ], }); Hooks Hooks let extensions step into tasks, including the built-in tasks for generating a model response, invoking a tool, or performing compaction. They can rewrite a request before it goes to the model, block or rewrite a tool call, replace a result, keep a run going, or write a summary themselves. A hook can run again after a crash, so a hook that makes a decision stores it in a memo: a small value stored with the task, where the first write wins. import { hook, ToolTask } from "@earendil-works/pi-durable" ; const Approval = defineExtension({ name: "approval" , hooks: [ hook(ToolTask, { beforeTool: async (call, api, context) =&gt; { if (call.name !== "deploy" ) return undefined ; // After a restart, the hook finds the stored answer instead of // asking again. let approved = await api.memo&lt;boolean&gt;( "approval:deploy" , context, ); approved ??= await api.memo( "approval:deploy" , await askInSlack(call), context, ); return approved ? undefined : { block: "Nobody approved the deploy." }; }, }), ], }); Several extensions can hook the same thing. Their hooks run as a chain, in the order the conversation selects the extensions, and each hook defines how its chain runs. beforeTool passes rewritten arguments down the chain, and the first block stops it. afterTool passes the result down the chain. onYield stops at the first hook that keeps the run going. Observers like afterResponse always run them all. A hook that throws is reported, and the chain continues, except in beforeTool , where a throw blocks the call. Tasks The harness runs conversations with built-in tasks: one for each model request, one for each tool call, and one for compaction. Extensions bring their own tasks and get the same machinery: a checkpoint after every step, timers that survive restarts, and waiting on other tasks. A checkout that splits the bill across several cards charges every card at once. If one card is declined, the other payments are aborted and refund themselves: import { defineTask, type TaskId } from "@earendil-works/pi-durable" ; const Payment = defineTask&lt;{ card: string }, { phase: "charge" }, string&gt;({ name: "shop.payment" , version: 1, initial: () =&gt; ({ phase: "charge" }), phases: { charge: async (task, runtime, context) =&gt; { // The key makes the charge idempotent: if a crash reruns this // phase, the card is only charged once. const charge = await bank.charge( task.input.card, `payment-${ task.id }` , ); await runtime.commit( () =&gt; ({ status: "terminal" , outcome: charge.ok ? { status: "completed" , result: charge.receipt } : { status: "failed" , error: { message: charge.error } }, }), context, ); }, }, // Another payment failed, or the checkout was cancelled: undo this one. abort: async (task, runtime, context) =&gt; { await bank.refund( `payment-${ task.id }` ); await runtime.commit( () =&gt; ({ status: "terminal" , outcome: { status: "aborted" } }), context, ); }, }); type CheckoutState = | { phase: "pay" } | { phase: "decide" ; payments: TaskId&lt;string&gt;[] }; const Checkout = defineTask&lt;{ cards: string[] }, CheckoutState, string&gt;({ name: "shop.checkout" , version: 1, initial: () =&gt; ({ phase: "pay" }), phases: { pay: async (task, runtime, context) =&gt; { await runtime.commit( async (tx) =&gt; { const payments: TaskId&lt;string&gt;[] = []; for ( const card of task.input.cards) { payments.push( await tx.createTask(Payment, { card }, { ownership: { kind: "task" , taskId: task.id }, }), ); } // Run no code until every payment is done. The first failed // payment aborts the others. return { status: "waiting" , checkpoint: { phase: "decide" , payments }, on: payments, policy: "failFast" , }; }, context); }, decide: async (task, runtime, context) =&gt; { const outcomes = await runtime.outcomes( task.state.checkpoint.payments, context, ); const paid = outcomes.every( (outcome) =&gt; outcome.status === "completed" , ); await runtime.commit( () =&gt; ({ status: "terminal" , outcome: paid ? { status: "completed" , result: "Order placed." } : { status: "failed" , error: { message: "A payment failed." }, }, }), context, ); }, }, abort: (_task, runtime, context) =&gt; runtime.commit( () =&gt; ({ status: "terminal" , outcome: { status: "aborted" } }), context, ), }); // The agent starts a checkout with a tool. const checkout = defineTool({ name: "checkout" , description: "Pay for the cart, split across several cards" , parameters: Type.Object({ cards: Type.Array(Type.String()) }), execute: async (args, api, context) =&gt; { // Owned by this call: aborting the call aborts the checkout and refunds // its payments. const owner = { ownership: { kind: "task" , taskId: api.taskId }, } as const ; const id = await api.createTask( Checkout, { cards: args.cards }, owner, context, ); const { outcome } = ( await api.waitForTask(id, context)).state; const text = outcome.status === "completed" ? outcome.result : outcome.status; return { content: [{ type : "text" , text }] }; }, }); registry.install(defineExtension({ name: "shop" , tools: [checkout], tasks: [Payment, Checkout], })); Tasks and conversations form one ownership tree. Aborting a task aborts what it owns, bottom-up, so every task cleans up its own effects first, and a task only finishes once the work it owns has finished. A subagent is the same pattern: a conversation owned by the tool call that started it. Tasks are foreground by default: they are part of the conversation's current work. The conversation is idle only once they are done, and aborting the conversation, for example when the user presses Esc, aborts them and everything they own. A background task belongs to the conversation, but not to its current work. The conversation goes idle while it runs, and an ordinary abort leaves it and everything it owns alone. That fits a subagent that should outlive the turn that started it, or a reminder that fires tomorrow. Aborting the task itself, or the conversation with { background: true } , still stops it. // Part of the current work: Esc aborts it, and the conversation waits for it. await api.createTask( Checkout, input, { ownership: { kind: "task" , taskId: api.taskId } }, context, ); // Side work: the conversation goes idle while it runs, and Esc leaves it alone. await api.createTask( Reminder, input, { ownership: { kind: "conversation" }, background: true }, context, ); Compaction We want long conversations to keep going without the agent stopping to summarize. In Pi Durable, compaction is a task like any other, and it runs while the conversation keeps going. When the context gets close to the model's limit, a background compaction summarizes the older messages, and the summary is placed at the next turn boundary. # pi-durable on Cloudflare

A working example of [`@earendil-works/pi-durable`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@earendil-works/pi-durable) running in a Cloudflare Durable Object.

Start with the [Pi Durable announcement](https://earendil.com/posts/pi-durable/) for the ideas behind the harness. This repository shows one way to put those ideas into a small, usable web application.

Pi Durable is experimental, so its APIs may still change.

## What you can try

- Create a shared chat session and open it in multiple browsers.
- Run several conversations at once and fork a conversation from an earlier message.
- Reconnect without losing committed transcripts or queued prompts.
- Schedule one-time or recurring follow-ups.
- Ask a search subagent about earlier conversations.
- Open Activity to inspect live task ownership, waits, sleeps, tool calls, and background work while conversations run.

This is a sample, not a production service. It intentionally has no authentication or rate limiting.

## Run it locally

You need Node.js 22.19 or newer, pnpm 11, and an OpenAI API key.

```sh
pnpm install
cp .dev.vars.example .dev.vars
```

Add your key to `.dev.vars`:

```dotenv
OPENAI_API_KEY=your-key
```

Then start the Worker and React client together:

```sh
pnpm dev
```

Open the local URL printed by Vite, create a session, and send a message. Open the session URL in another browser to try the multiplayer flow.

## Where to look

The shortest path through the project is:

- [`src/chat.ts`](src/chat.ts) defines the models, extensions, tools, and default agent.
- [`src/session.ts`](src/session.ts) hosts the harness with Pi Durable's built-in Durable Object SQLite storage and connects it to Cloudflare's native hibernating WebSockets and alarms. Each socket watches one conversation's view (`Conversation.watch()`): the server sends its first value, then its changes as Chord operations, and pages older entries on request.
- [`src/tools.ts`](src/tools.ts), [`src/schedule.ts`](src/schedule.ts), and [`src/search.ts`](src/search.ts) contain the example tools and tasks.
- [`src/client/`](src/client/) is the React client. It applies the operations to each conversation's view, keeps the whole transcript with Pi Durable's `ConversationTranscript`, and renders the result: entries, and `pi.live` for the run, the streamed answer, tool progress, and failures.
- [`test/`](test/) covers application flows including restart recovery, scheduling, forks, and inboxes. Pi Durable tests its built-in Cloudflare storage adapter inside a Durable Object itself.

The code is the documentation for this integration. In particular, the tests are useful examples of restart behavior, scheduling, forks, and inboxes.

## Commands

```sh
pnpm dev        # local development
pnpm test       # test suite
pnpm check      # formatting, types, build, and deploy dry run
pnpm build      # production build
pnpm preview    # preview the production build locally
```

## Deploy

Authenticate Wrangler, store the API key as a Worker secret, then deploy:

```sh
pnpm exec wrangler login
pnpm exec wrangler secret put OPENAI_API_KEY
pnpm deploy
```

Before exposing a deployment, add authentication, authorization, and rate limiting. Anyone who can reach this sample can create sessions that use your model credentials.

## Further reading

- [Pi Durable announcement](https://earendil.com/posts/pi-durable/)
- [pi-durable package documentation](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/tree/main/packages/durable)
- [pi-durable examples](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/tree/main/packages/durable/test/examples)
- [Cloudflare Durable Objects](https://developers.cloudflare.com/durable-objects/)</result>
